source_claim_sections:
Example

At $e=2$ one has $[3]=q^2+1+q^{-2}$ and the cubic relation
$S_X=X_0^3X_1-[3]X_0^2X_1X_0+[3]X_0X_1X_0^2-X_1X_0^3=0$ for $X=E,F$, products
acting right to left. The four $E$ compositions all vanish on
$\varnothing,1,2,11$ by size, so only size $\ge4$ inputs test the identity. The
four $F$ compositions all vanish on $\varnothing,1,3,111$. On $2$ the ordered
four outputs are $([3]A,A,0,0)$ with $A=(q^{-2}+1)|321\rangle$; on $11$ they are
$([3]B,B,0,0)$ with $B=(q^{-1}+q)|321\rangle$, giving cancellation. On $21$ they
are $(0,C,D,[3](D-C))$ with
$C=[2]\bigl(|52\rangle+q|511\rangle+q^2|421\rangle+q|3211\rangle+q^2|31111\rangle+q^3|22111\rangle\bigr)$
and $D-C=[2]\bigl(|421\rangle+q|331\rangle+q^3|3211\rangle+q^2|322\rangle\bigr)$.
A nontrivial $E$ check on $321$ has four outputs $(0,0,Z,[3]Z)$ with
$Z=(1+q^2)|11\rangle+(q^{-1}+q)|2\rangle$. All displayed Serre sums vanish,
whereas $F_0F_1|1\rangle=|3\rangle+q|111\rangle$ and $F_1F_0|1\rangle=0$ show
the colors do not commute.
source_proof_sections:
Verification

1.1 The vanishing cases. Every $E$ monomial removes four cells, so all four outputs on $\varnothing,1,2,11$ vanish. For $F$ on $\varnothing$, $F_1\varnothing=0$ and $F_0\varnothing=1$, $F_0 1=0$; these kill all four compositions. On $1,3,111$, the three compositions with a rightmost $F_0$ vanish because $F_0$ kills each input. For the remaining $F_0^3F_1$, the node formulas give $F_0^2F_1|1\rangle=0$, $F_0^2F_1|3\rangle=(q^{-2}+1)|321\rangle$, and $F_0^2F_1|111\rangle=(q^{-1}+q)|321\rangle$; in both latter cases $F_0|321\rangle=0$ since it has no addable $0$-node. Thus each of the four $F$ outputs on the stated boundary inputs is zero. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The size-$2$ cancellations. Starting from $|2\rangle$ and applying the four ordered compositions via [F1] gives the first output as $[3](q^{-2}+1)|3,2,1\rangle$, the second as $(q^{-2}+1)|3,2,1\rangle$, and the last two $0$: indeed the coefficient of $|321\rangle$ in the leading output is $q^{-4}+2q^{-2}+2+q^2=[3](q^{-2}+1)$ and the other outputs contribute the same multiple of the middle term; cancelling gives $0$. The same computation from $|1,1\rangle$ gives outputs $([3]B,B,0,0)$ with $B=(q^{-1}+q)|321\rangle$ because the coefficient is $q^{-3}+2q^{-1}+2q+q^3=[3](q^{-1}+q)$. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

2.2 Noncommutation. Direct evaluation gives $F_0F_1|1\rangle=|3\rangle+q|1,1,1\rangle$ and $F_1F_0|1\rangle=0$, since $F_0|1\rangle=0$; hence the ordinary generators do not commute. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 The size-$3$ cancellations. From $|2,1\rangle$ the second composition yields the common term $C$, the third yields $D$, and the fourth yields $[3](D-C)$, so the sum contributes $[3](-C+D-(D-C))=0$ coefficientwise; from $|3,2,1\rangle$, applying the $E$-compositions gives the last output $[3]Z$ with the stated $Z$, and the first two outputs vanish, while the third output is $Z$; the sum vanishes. [step 2.1, F1, algebra]

4.1 Conclusion. The displayed finite chains exhibit the double-edge Serre cancellation on $2,11,21$ and the $E$ cancellation on $321$, with the $[3]$ coefficients $q^2+1+q^{-2}$; the general relation including the colour swap is proved by the independent rank-one Serre lemma, so no finite diagnostic is promoted to a universal proof. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, F2] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Example

At $e=2$ the ambient lower basis in degrees $\le3$ is
$\varnothing\mapsto|\varnothing\rangle$, $1\mapsto|1\rangle$,
$11\mapsto|11\rangle$, $2\mapsto|2\rangle+q|11\rangle$,
$111\mapsto|111\rangle$, $3\mapsto|3\rangle+q|111\rangle$,
$21\mapsto|21\rangle$. The basic labels in these degrees are
$\varnothing,1,2,3,21$ (not $11$ or $111$). In degree $4$, rows and columns
ordered $4,31,22,211,1111$, the full lower transition matrix
$D$ (column $=G$-label, row $=$ standard shape) is

$$\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0&0\\q&1&0&0&0\\0&q&1&0&0\\q&q^2&q&1&0\\q^2&0&0&q&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its basic columns are $4$ and $31$. All entries lie in $\mathbb Z[q]$, the
diagonal is $1$, and off-diagonal entries lie in $q\mathbb Z[q]$, with the
proved dominance and core bounds. The apparent transpose-conjugation identity
holds accidentally for the displayed degrees $\le3$ but is **false** generally:
$d_{(211),(4)}=q$ whereas $d_{(1111),(31)}=0$. The source symmetry concerns the
bar transition matrix, not $D$. The ambient bar-fixed $G(111)$ lies outside the
basic module; no arbitrary bar-fixed combination need lie in one isotypic
summand.
source_proof_sections:
Verification

1.1 The degrees $\le3$. Solving the triangular bar equations degree by degree with the reversal bar: in degree $2$ the only correction of $2$ is $q\,11$; in degree $3$ the partition $21$ is the only shape whose residue multiset forces no correction and $3$ receives the correction $q\,111$; the remaining shapes are bar-fixed. This gives the displayed degree-$\le3$ elements, and the basic labels are the $2$-regular ones, namely $\varnothing,1,2,3,21$, with $11$ and $111$ non-regular. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The degree-four bar calculation. The finite reversal formula of [F1], at any cutoff longer than four, and straightening give $\psi|4\rangle=|4\rangle+(q-q^{-1})|31\rangle+(q^{-2}-1)|22\rangle+(q^2-1)|1111\rangle$, $\psi|31\rangle=|31\rangle+(q-q^{-1})|22\rangle+(q^2-1)|211\rangle$, $\psi|22\rangle=|22\rangle+(q-q^{-1})|211\rangle+(q^{-2}-1)|1111\rangle$, $\psi|211\rangle=|211\rangle+(q-q^{-1})|1111\rangle$ and $\psi|1111\rangle=|1111\rangle$. Substituting these five formulas, with coefficient bar, verifies the displayed columns $G(4)=|4\rangle+q|31\rangle+q|211\rangle+q^2|1111\rangle$, $G(31)=|31\rangle+q|22\rangle+q^2|211\rangle$, $G(22)=|22\rangle+q|211\rangle$, $G(211)=|211\rangle+q|1111\rangle$ and $G(1111)=|1111\rangle$: each is bar fixed with its stated leading residue and coefficients in $q\mathbb Z[q]$. Uniqueness in [F1] therefore identifies them with the lower lifts. The basic labels are the regular shapes $4,31$, and the nonzero positions visibly respect dominance. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra]

3.1 The false transpose symmetry. Conjugation of partitions sends $211\mapsto31$ and $4\mapsto1111$, so the transpose-conjugation equality would require $d_{(211),(4)}=d_{(1111),(31)}$; but the degree-$4$ matrix gives $d_{(211),(4)}=q$ and $d_{(1111),(31)}=0$. Hence the equality fails in general; the source's symmetry statement concerns the bar transition matrix $A$, not the lower matrix $D$. [step 2.1, F2, algebra]

4.1 Conclusion. The displayed elements are the actual lower global basis elements in degrees $\le4$, their coefficients are integral and dominance-triangular, the basic columns are the regular labels, and the naive transpose symmetry of $D$ is refuted by the explicit pair. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Statement

Work over $\mathbb Q(q)$ with a symmetrizable Cartan datum of type $A$ as in
[[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]], put $q_i=q^{d_i}$ and let
$B$ be a unital $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra equipped with elements
$E_i,F_i,K_h^{\pm1}$ ($i\in I$, $h\in P^\vee$) satisfying the toral and
toral-action relations and the mixed commutators
$E_iF_j-F_jE_i=\delta_{ij}(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$ of
[[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]; let $W$ be a $B$-module with a chosen integral label grading on which $K_h$ acts by $q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle}$ on $W_\mu$, and $E_i,F_i$ shift labels by $\pm\alpha_i$. Assume that $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on $W$ for every $i$ (rank-one integrability). Then the negative quantum Serre sums

$$\sum_{r=0}^{1-a_{ij}}(-1)^r\binom{1-a_{ij}}{r}_iF_i^{1-a_{ij}-r}F_jF_i^r=0\qquad(i\ne j)$$

vanish as operators on $W$, and, by the Chevalley interchange
$E_i\leftrightarrow F_i$, $K_h\leftrightarrow K_{-h}$, so do the positive sums
$\sum_{r}(-1)^r\binom{1-a_{ij}}{r}_iE_i^{1-a_{ij}-r}E_jE_i^r$. In particular the
$e=2$ cubic sums with $a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ hold. No Serre relation is assumed.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

**Proof technique:** compute the iterated adjoint action of $F_i$ on $F_j$ by the Gaussian binomial formula, show it vanishes beyond the rank-one string bound, and read the Serre sum off the surviving coefficient.

1.1 The adjoint action of $F_i$ on operators is $\operatorname{ad}(T)=F_iT-K_iTK_i^{-1}F_i$, and on $T=F_j$ one has $\operatorname{ad}^n(F_j)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}(-1)^rq^{r(m-n+1)}\binom{n}{r}_iF_i^{n-r}F_jF_i^r$ for every $n\ge0$, where $m=-a_{ij}$ is the $K_i$-weight of $F_j$ from [F1]. The case $n=0$ is the definition; the induction step multiplies the formula for $n$ on the left by $F_i$ and conjugates the rightmost factor, using $K_iF_jK_i^{-1}=q^mF_j$ and $K_iF_i^rK_i^{-1}=q^{-2r}F_i^r$ to move the toral elements, and the coefficient identity $\binom{n+1}{r}_i=q^{r}\binom{n}{r}_i+q^{r-n-1}\binom{n}{r-1}_i$ of [F4] (with $q$ replaced by $q_i=q$); the powers of $q$ combine to $q^{r(m-n)}$. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 The finite Hom-space string bound. Fix $w\in W$ and let $U$ be its finite-dimensional rank-one submodule: for a homogeneous vector take the span of $F_i^aE_i^bw$, with finitely many $b$ by local nilpotence of $E_i$ and finitely many $a$ for each $b$ by local nilpotence of $F_i$; the rank-one commutator in [F2] makes this span stable. For a general vector sum the finitely many such spaces of its label components. Choose a finite basis of $U$ and let $U'$ be the sum of the finite rank-one submodules generated by its $F_j$-images. Then $F_j|_U$ belongs to the finite type-one rank-one module $\operatorname{Hom}(U,U')$, with operators $\mathcal K(T)=K_i'TK_i^{-1}$, $\mathcal E(T)=(E_i'T-TE_i)K_i$ and $\mathcal F(T)=F_i'T-\mathcal K(T)F_i$. Substitution of the rank-one relations verifies $\mathcal K\mathcal E\mathcal K^{-1}=q^2\mathcal E$, $\mathcal K\mathcal F\mathcal K^{-1}=q^{-2}\mathcal F$ and $[\mathcal E,\mathcal F]=(\mathcal K-\mathcal K^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$. Its integral weights lie in a finite set, so both weight-shifting operators are nilpotent. For $T=F_j|_U$, [F1] gives $\mathcal K(T)=q^mT$ and $\mathcal E(T)=0$. The highest-vector endpoint calculation in [F2] (or the rank-one proof of [F3], which uses no Serre relations) therefore gives $\mathcal F^{m+1}T=0$. Its expansion is exactly step 1.1 restricted to $U$, so $\operatorname{ad}^{m+1}(F_j)w=0$. No preservation of $U$ by $F_j$ is assumed. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The negative Serre sum vanishes. Put $n:=m+1=1-a_{ij}$. At $n=m+1$ the exponent in the expansion of step 1.1 is $r(m-n+1)=0$, so step 2.1 gives $0=\operatorname{ad}^{n}(F_j)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}(-1)^r\binom{n}{r}_iF_i^{n-r}F_jF_i^r$; as an operator identity on each $U$ containing $w$, hence on every vector $w\in W$ this is exactly the negative Serre sum. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 The positive Serre sum vanishes. The Chevalley interchange of [F5] preserves all toral, toral-action and mixed relations used above and exchanges the roles of the $E$'s and $F$'s, so applying the argument of steps 1.1--3.1 to the image operators gives $\sum_{r=0}^{1-a_{ij}}(-1)^r\binom{1-a_{ij}}{r}_iE_i^{1-a_{ij}-r}E_jE_i^r=0$ on every weight vector, hence as operators. [step 3.1, F5, given, algebra]

5.1 Conclusion. Under only the toral, toral-action, mixed-commutator and rank-one-integrability hypotheses, both quantum Serre sums of order $1-a_{ij}$ vanish, for every pair $i\ne j$ of the cyclic affine type $A$ datum, the cubic case included; no Serre relation was assumed. [step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Statement

Keep the conventions of the charge-$M$ Fock space
[[def-semi-infinite-q-wedge-fock-space-and-q-adic-topology]]. Normal wedges are
bijective with partitions through $i_k=M+\lambda_k-k+1$; in charge $0$ the
vacuum is the empty partition. The stable finite-prefix action defines linear
endomorphisms $F_i,E_i,K_i,K_d$ of $F^{(0)}$ by

$$F_i|\lambda\rangle=\sum_{\text{addable }\gamma\text{ of residue }i}q^{A_i^r-R_i^r}\,|\lambda+\gamma\rangle,\qquad E_i|\mu\rangle=\sum_{\text{removable }\gamma\text{ of residue }i}q^{-(A_i^l-R_i^l)}\,|\mu-\gamma\rangle,$$

where for $F_i$ the counts are taken in the smaller diagram $\lambda$ and count
addable/removable $i$-nodes strictly to the right of the added node (higher
content), and for $E_i$ the counts are taken in the smaller diagram $\mu-\gamma$
and count nodes strictly to the left of the removed node (lower content), with
the removed node excluded; all sums are finite. The toral operators act by
$K_i|\lambda\rangle=q^{N_i(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$ with $N_i$ the
addable-minus-removable count, and $K_d|\lambda\rangle=q^{-m_0(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$;
the size $|\lambda|$ is a separate grading. Charge $M$ replaces the residues by
content $+M$ and $K_d$ by $\Omega_M(d)-m_0$.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

**Proof technique:** evaluate the finite-prefix coproduct on a chosen entry, translate collisions into corner additions, and control the artificial boundary by renormalising the cutoff.

1.1 The bijection and finiteness of the node sums. The map $\lambda\mapsto(i_k)_{k\ge1}$ with $i_k=M+\lambda_k-k+1$ is a bijection onto normal semi-infinite words because $\lambda$ is weakly decreasing and eventually zero, and $i_k$ is strictly decreasing and eventually equal to the ground tail; a partition of size $n$ has at most $n+1$ addable nodes and at most $n$ removable nodes, so both sums in the statement are finite. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 The $F_i$ formula. On a prefix of length $N$ containing the support of $|\lambda\rangle$, the coproduct action of $F_i$ shifts a selected entry $i_k$ to $i_k+1$, provided $i_k\equiv i$; if $i_k+1=i_{k-1}$ the resulting term has a collision and vanishes by the wedge relations, and otherwise the shift is exactly the addition of the corner cell $(k,\lambda_k+1)$ of residue $i$ by [F3]. The coefficient is the product of the prefix $K$-eigenvalues of the finite coproduct, which is $q^{A_i^r-R_i^r}$: a frozen doubly occupied $i$-pair contributes net weight $0$, and the singly occupied $i$-pairs are exactly the other addable and removable $i$-corners, ordered by content, contributing $+1$ for each addable corner strictly to the right (higher content) of the added node and $-1$ for each removable one. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.2 The $E_i$ formula. For $E_i$ the finite-prefix coproduct shifts an entry with $i_k\equiv i+1$ to $i_k-1$; if it collides the term is zero, and otherwise it deletes the corner cell $(k,\lambda_k)$ of residue $i$, whose smaller diagram is $\mu-\gamma$. The suffix $K^{-1}$-weight contributes the addable and removable $i$-corners of $\mu-\gamma$ strictly to the left (lower content) of the removed node; the single artificial boundary pair at the cutoff contributes $q^{\delta_{i\equiv M-N}}$ to the finite $E_i$ coefficient, which is cancelled by the factor $q^{-\delta_{i\equiv M-N}}$ in the renormalised operator $q^{-\delta_{i\equiv M-N}}E_i$. The artificial removal at the cutoff duplicates the first appended ground entry and vanishes; after one more ground entry is appended, the same cancellation removes the changed boundary factor. Thus the renormalised operator is cutoff-independent and defines the stable limit by [F2]. The sign is negative because $E_i$ shifts down in the wedge. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 The toral normalization. On a normal prefix of length $N$ extending past the partition's nonzero rows, the finite $K_i$ exponent is $N_i(\lambda)-\delta_{i\equiv M-N}$: the genuine corner pairs give the count, and the cutoff leaves one artificial occupied bottom of the pair $(M-N,M-N+1)$. Therefore the stabilized operator is $q^{\delta_{i\equiv M-N}}K_i^{[N]}$ after tail attachment and acts by $q^{N_i(\lambda)}$. For the degree torus, normalize the finite action by $q^{\Omega_{M-N}(d)}K_d^{[N]}$. The vacuum recurrence gives $\Omega_M=\Omega_{M-N}+\sum_{k=1}^N\mathrm{wt}(u_{M-k+1})$. Each admissible row shift adds a cell of content plus charge $i$ and changes the vector weight by $-\alpha_i$; hence the normalized label is $\Omega_M-\sum_{\mathrm{cells}}\alpha_{c-r+M}$. Since $\langle\alpha_i,d\rangle=\delta_{i0}$, the degree eigenvalue is $q^{\Omega_M(d)-m_0(\lambda)}$, equal to $q^{-m_0(\lambda)}$ in charge zero. These normalized operators are independent of the cutoff. [step 2.1, step 2.2, F3, given, algebra]

4.1 Conclusion. Normal wedges are bijective with partitions, and the stable finite-prefix action gives the displayed finite node formulas for $F_i,E_i,K_i,K_d$ before any relation or crystal statement is invoked. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Statement

The constructed node operators on **all** partition vectors make the charge-$0$
partition Fock space $F$ into a $P$-graded integrable module for
$U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_e)$ with the fixed coproduct and the cyclic Cartan
datum: all toral commutation rules and mixed commutators
$[E_i,F_j]=\delta_{ij}(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ hold, and both quantum Serre
sums vanish, including the cubic $e=2$ case with
$a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ and $[3]=q^2+1+q^{-2}$. Each color acts on finite Boolean
cubes, and $F_i,E_i$ change the $P$-weight by $\mp\alpha_i$. Ordinary standard
coefficients may have $q^{-1}$ poles; normalized Kashiwara lattice stability is
a separate statement.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

**Proof technique:** check the toral rules and mixed commutators locally on overlapping cubes, then invoke the rank-one Serre engine.

1.1 The toral rules. By [F1] the $K_i$ are diagonal in the partition basis and $F_j,E_j$ shift the weight by $\mp\alpha_j$; hence $K_iE_jK_i^{-1}=q^{\langle\alpha_j,h_i\rangle}E_j=q^{a_{ij}}E_j$ and $K_iF_jK_i^{-1}=q^{-a_{ij}}F_j$, the $K$'s commute, and the central product acts by $q$ by [F4]. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 The mixed commutators. For $i\ne j$, use the genuine finite-wedge module of [[thm-normally-ordered-q-wedges-form-a-basis]], obtained from the vector module by the coproduct of [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]] and a quantum-group-stable kernel. Its operators satisfy $[E_i^{[N]},F_j^{[N]}]=0$, where $[N]$ denotes the prefix length, not a divided power. For a given partition choose $N$ beyond the nonvacuum rows of that partition and all its finitely many one- and two-step node outputs. The stable-prefix formula gives $F_j=F_j^{[N]}$ after tail attachment and $E_i=q^{-\delta_{i\equiv -N}}E_i^{[N]}$ after tail attachment, with the same scalar on both intermediate diagrams. Thus $[E_i,F_j]$ is the image of $q^{-\delta_{i\equiv -N}}[E_i^{[N]},F_j^{[N]}]$ and is zero. No relation for the infinite module is assumed in this finite calculation. For $i=j$, the exact tensor cubes in [F2] give $[E_i,F_i]=(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

3.1 The Serre sums. By steps 1.1 and 2.1 the node operators satisfy every toral rule and every mixed commutator, and by [F2] each single-color action is integrable; the rank-one Serre engine [F3] then forces both quantum Serre sums for every pair $i\ne j$, the $e=2$ cubic case included. No Serre relation was used before this point. [step 2.1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

4.1 Conclusion. The node operators satisfy all defining relations of the affine algebra with the fixed coproduct, each color acts on finite cubes (integrability), the weight shifts are $\mp\alpha_i$, and ordinary coefficients with negative powers of $q$ are kept separate from the normalized lattice statement. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Statement

The stable prefix operators on the charge-$M$ algebraic wedge direct limit give
a well-defined integrable action of the affine quantum algebra, proved from the
node formulas and all defining relations of
[[thm-the-fock-space-node-formulas-satisfy-the-quantum-affine-relations]].
Boundary-normalized infinite coproduct expressions converge $q$-adically and in this type-A model
have finite stabilised outputs; no two-sided-unbounded evaluation statement is
imported. On the vacuum $E_i\varnothing=0$, $F_i$ creates the single node of
residue $M$ and $K_i$ acts by $q^{\delta_{i\equiv M}}$. The wedge product of a
finite prefix with its correctly charged tail is $U_q$-linear with the fixed
formulas

$$E(v\wedge u)=Ev\wedge K_i^{-1}u+v\wedge Eu,\qquad F(v\wedge u)=Fv\wedge u+K_iv\wedge Fu .$$

With the declared use of the Axiom of Choice only in the general integrable
decomposition, the finite-weight upper cone of $F$ is a locally weight-finite
direct sum of simple integrable highest weight modules; completeness does not
mean finitely many constituents.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

**Proof technique:** show each coproduct expression stabilises on a finite prefix, check the wedge product formula on the finite prefix, and apply semisimplicity with the declared choice.

1.1 Stabilized, normalized coproducts. For a charge-$M$ partition choose a prefix of length $N$ extending beyond its nonvacuum rows and all finitely many node outputs. The stable-prefix computation in [F2] uses $F_i^{[N]}$, $q^{-\delta_{i\equiv M-N}}E_i^{[N]}$, $q^{\delta_{i\equiv M-N}}K_i^{[N]}$ and $q^{\Omega_{M-N}(d)}K_d^{[N]}$, followed by tail attachment. Here $[N]$ denotes the finite coproduct action. Each has the cutoff-independent node value proved in that supplier; any deeper individual insertion vanishes by [F1]. Thus these normalized expressions stabilize exactly and converge in the separated $q$-adic topology. The unnormalized finite $E_i$ and toral coproducts are not claimed to converge. For charge $M$, the node coefficients are the charge-zero coefficients with colors shifted by $M$, so the mixed commutator and Serre proofs of [F2] apply under that relabelling. The full toral operators are assigned by the displayed label weights, which shift by $\pm\alpha_i$ and therefore satisfy every toral-action relation, including the degree direction. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The wedge product formulas. Split a sufficiently deep finite prefix at length $r$, with the right part representing a charge-$(M-r)$ tail $u$. Its artificial boundary is again $M-N$. Write $b=\delta_{i\equiv M-N}$. The normalized right torus is $K_i u=q^bK_i^{[N-r]}u$, and its normalized raising operator is $E_i u=q^{-b}E_i^{[N-r]}u$. Multiplying the finite split coproduct by $q^{-b}$ therefore gives $E_i(v\wedge u)=E_iv\wedge K_i^{-1}u+v\wedge E_iu$. The finite lowering coproduct needs no scalar correction, giving $F_i(v\wedge u)=F_iv\wedge u+K_iv\wedge F_iu$. For the torus the two labels add, since $\Omega_M=\sum_{k=1}^r\mathrm{wt}(u_{M-k+1})+\Omega_{M-r}$ by the vacuum recurrence; the degree normalization agrees at the common cutoff as well. Stabilization from step 1.1 and linearity transport these finite identities through the local wedge quotient, proving quantum-group linearity. On the vacuum the only addable node has residue $M$, all raising operators vanish, and $K_i$ acts by $q^{\delta_{i\equiv M}}$. [step 1.1, F2, algebra]

3.1 Integrability and decomposition. For a fixed color, [F2] puts each basis vector in a finite two-vertex tensor cube; a vector is a finite linear combination, so both generators of that color are locally nilpotent on it. The charge-$M$ label is $\Omega_M-\sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$, so the support lies in the single downward cone $\Omega_M-Q^+$. Since the simple roots of the full affine datum are independent, a weight fixes all residue counts $m_i$ and hence the size $\sum_i m_i$; only finitely many partitions have that size, proving finite-dimensional label spaces. Thus all the finite-cone and finite-weight hypotheses of [F3] hold, and $F$ is a locally weight-finite direct sum of simple integrable highest weight modules. Choice enters only through [F3]. Characters and multiplicities are computed later from the actual crystal highest vertices. [step 2.1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

4.1 Conclusion. The stable prefix operators give a well-defined integrable affine action on the charge-$M$ Fock space with the displayed wedge product formulas, $q$-adic convergence and finite stabilisation, and the finite-weight upper cone is a locally weight-finite direct sum of simple integrable highest weight modules, with the Axiom of Choice used only as declared. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

The stable-prefix computation in [F2] uses $F_i^{[N]}$, $q^{-\delta_{i\equiv M-N}}E_i^{[N]}$, $q^{\delta_{i\equiv M-N}}K_i^{[N]}$ and $q^{\Omega_{M-N}(d)}K_d^{[N]}$, followed by tail attachment. Here $[N]$ denotes the finite coproduct action. Each has the cutoff-independent node value proved in that supplier; any deeper individual insertion vanishes by [F1]. Thus these normalized expressions stabilize exactly and converge in the separated $q$-adic topology. The unnormalized finite $E_i$ and toral coproducts are not claimed to converge. For charge $M$, the node coefficients are the charge-zero coefficients with colors shifted by $M$, so the mixed commutator and Serre proofs of [F2] apply under that relabelling. The full toral operators are assigned by the displayed label weights, which shift by $\pm\alpha_i$ and therefore satisfy every toral-action relation, including the degree direction. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The wedge product formulas. Split a sufficiently deep finite prefix at length $r$, with the right part representing a charge-$(M-r)$ tail $u$. Its artificial boundary is again $M-N$. Write $b=\delta_{i\equiv M-N}$. The normalized right torus is $K_i u=q^bK_i^{[N-r]}u$, and its normalized raising operator is $E_i u=q^{-b}E_i^{[N-r]}u$. Multiplying the finite split coproduct by $q^{-b}$ therefore gives $E_i(v\wedge u)=E_iv\wedge K_i^{-1}u+v\wedge E_iu$. The finite lowering coproduct needs no scalar correction, giving $F_i(v\wedge u)=F_iv\wedge u+K_iv\wedge F_iu$. Stabilization from step 1.1 and linearity transport these finite identities through the local wedge quotient, proving quantum-group linearity. On the vacuum the only addable node has residue $M$, all raising operators vanish, and $K_i$ acts by $q^{\delta_{i\equiv M}}$. [step 1.1, F2, algebra]

[step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Statement refuted

In the rank-one case $n=2$ the element $\rho':=x_1+x_2$ is a degree-two element
of $S$ with $\rho'(\alpha_s^\vee)=0$, so it is not strictly dominant. Its action
on the reduced rank-one Soergel module is zero: $\rho'=e_1=x_1+x_2$ is
$s$-invariant and of positive degree, and $x_1+x_2=1\cdot e_1$ acts on the right
basis element $\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}$ as the right action by an element of
$S_+$, hence $\rho'\cdot\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}=0$; a fortiori it cannot map
$(\overline{B_s})^{-1}=\mathbb R\,\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}$ isomorphically to
$(\overline{B_s})^{1}$. Therefore for $\rho'$ the hard Lefschetz property fails
(the map on the $-1$ degree is the zero map), even though $\rho'$ is a symmetric
degree-two endomorphism of the reduced module; the same failure occurs for every
degree-two element with $\rho'(\alpha_s^\vee)=0$. Consequently the hard Lefschetz and Hodge-Riemann conclusions do not hold
for arbitrary degree-two elements when strict dominance is omitted. This does
not assert that every Lefschetz element is strictly dominant.
source_proof_sections:
Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct computation in the rank-one reduced module.

1.1 **Non-dominance.** The reflection $s$ exchanges $x_1$ and $x_2$, so $\rho'=x_1+x_2$ is $s$-invariant and $\rho'(\alpha^\vee)=(x_1+x_2,x_1-x_2)=1-1=0$ in the standard form of the coordinate normalization; in particular $\rho'$ is not strictly dominant. [given, F1]

2.1 **The left action of $\rho'$ equals its right action.** Since $\rho'\in S^{s}$, the balanced tensor relation gives $\rho'\otimes1=1\otimes\rho'$ in $B_s$; hence for every $b\in B_s$ the left multiplication $\rho'\cdot b$ equals the right multiplication $b\cdot\rho'$: indeed both actions are $S$-linear and the identity holds on the two basis elements $c_{\mathrm{id}}$ (where $\rho'\cdot c_{\mathrm{id}}=\rho'\otimes1=1\otimes\rho'=c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdot\rho'$) and $c_s$ (where both equal $c_s\rho'$ by [F1]). [step 1.1, given, F1]

3.1 **The operator vanishes on the reduced module.** By step 2.1, $\rho'\cdot c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdot\rho'=1\otimes\rho'$ lies in $B_sS_+$, since it is the right product of $c_{\mathrm{id}}=1\otimes1$ with $\rho'\in S_+$; by [F2] its class in $\overline{B_s}$ is zero, so $\rho'\cdot\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}=0$. Similarly $\rho'\cdot c_s=c_s\cdot\rho'=c_s\rho'$ lies in $B_sS_+$ and reduces to zero. Since $\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}$ and $\overline{c_s}$ span $\overline{B_s}$, the induced operator $L=\rho'\cdot(-)$ is the zero endomorphism of $\overline{B_s}$. [step 2.1, F1, F2]

4.1 **Failure of hard Lefschetz.** The reduced module has $\dim(\overline{B_s})^{-1}=\dim(\overline{B_s})^{1}=1$ with bases $\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}$ and $\overline{c_s}$. The degree-one Lefschetz map $L:(\overline{B_s})^{-1}\to(\overline{B_s})^{1}$ is zero by step 3.1, hence not an isomorphism, and hard Lefschetz fails for $L$ in the sense of [F3]. The bottom Lefschetz form $\langle-,L(-)\rangle$ is likewise identically zero, so the Hodge-Riemann relations with any nonzero sign also fail. [step 3.1, F3]

5.1 **The general degree-two case.** Let $\rho''=ax_1+bx_2$ satisfy $\rho''(\alpha^\vee)=a-b=0$; then $a=b$ and $\rho''=a\rho'$ is a scalar multiple of $\rho'$. If $a=0$ the operator is trivially zero; if $a\ne0$ the same computation as in steps 2.1-4.1 applies because invariance and positivity of degree are unaffected by the scalar. Hence every degree-two element with vanishing evaluation on $\alpha_s^\vee$ yields the zero operator on the reduced rank-one module and fails hard Lefschetz. This proves the claimed failure and shows that allowing arbitrary degree-two elements invalidates the conclusion; no choice principle is used. [step 4.1] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Example

For $n=3$ identify the centered reduced longest-element module with $C(3)$, where $C=\mathbb R[x_1,x_2,x_3]/(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ has dimensions $1,2,2,1$ in degrees $0,2,4,6$, so that the centered degrees are $-3,-1,1,3$. For every strictly dominant $\rho$ hard Lefschetz is the pair of isomorphisms $\rho^3:C(3)^{-3}\to C(3)^3$ and $\rho:C(3)^{-1}\to C(3)^1$. The primitive spaces used in the Hodge-Riemann relations are $P^{-3}=C(3)^{-3}$ of dimension one and $P^{-1}=\ker(\rho^2:C(3)^{-1}\to C(3)^3)$ of dimension one; their Lefschetz forms are respectively positive and negative definite, and the primitive decomposition consists of one length-four $\rho$-string and one length-two $\rho$-string. For an explicit strictly dominant choice let $x=x_1$, $y=x_2$, $x_3=-x-y$, $\rho=x_1-x_3=2x+y$ and normalize $\operatorname{Tr}(x^2y)=1$. Then $C=\mathbb R[x,y]/(x^2+xy+y^2,x^3)$, with basis $1;x,y;x^2,xy;x^2y$; the $\rho$-map from degree $2$ to degree $4$ has the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $\rho^3(1)=6x^2y$, $P^{-1}=\mathbb Ry$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(y\rho y)=-2$. These computations verify hard Lefschetz and the primitive signs directly in rank two.
source_proof_sections:
Verification

**Proof technique:** direct; elimination of the linear invariant, reduction to a two-variable model, and explicit matrix and trace computations in both the special and the general dominant chamber.

**Given:** The coinvariant algebra $C=\mathbb R[x_1,x_2,x_3]/(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and the identification with the centered reduced module of $B_{w_0}$ ([[ex-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-s-three-as-the-longest-soergel-bimodule]]), the operator $\rho\cdot(-)$ of left multiplication by a strictly dominant degree-two element and the trace normalization ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]], [[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]]), and the hard-Lefschetz and Hodge-Riemann dictionary with the sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ for lowest degree $-d$ ([[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]], [[lem-hard-lefschetz-implies-primitive-decomposition]]).

[F1] The centered module $C(3)$ has lowest degree $-3$, graded dimensions $1,2,2,1$ in degrees $-3,-1,1,3$ and a non-degenerate invariant form normalized by the positive bottom value; for it, hard Lefschetz is $\rho^3:C^{-3}\to C^3$ together with $\rho:C^{-1}\to C^1$, and the standard sign in degree $-i$ is $(-1)^{(3-i)/2}$, so the primitive space $P^{-1}\subset C^{-1}$ must be negative definite and $P^{-3}=C^{-3}$ positive definite ([[ex-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-s-three-as-the-longest-soergel-bimodule]], [[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]]).

[F2] In the quotient the relations $e_1=e_2=e_3=0$ hold and, after the substitution $x_3=-x-y$, are equivalent to $x^2+xy+y^2=0$ and $x^3=0$; the reduction of the intersection form is the standard top trace with $\operatorname{Tr}(x^2y)=1$, and $C$ is spanned by the six monomials of the display ([[ex-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-s-three-as-the-longest-soergel-bimodule]]; the trace identification is checked in step 2.1).

1.1 **The two-variable model.** Put $x=x_1$, $y=x_2$ and $x_3=-x-y$. Then $e_1=x+y+x_3=0$, while $e_2=x_1x_2+x_1x_3+x_2x_3=xy+x(-x-y)+y(-x-y)=-(x^2+xy+y^2)$ and $e_3=x_1x_2x_3=-x^2y-xy^2$; hence the coinvariant ideal is generated by $x^2+xy+y^2$ and $x^2y+xy^2$, and since $x^3=x(x^2+xy+y^2)-x^2y-xy^2$ the second relation can be replaced by $x^3=0$, giving $C=\mathbb R[x,y]/(x^2+xy+y^2,x^3)$. The monomials $1;x,y;x^2,xy;x^2y$ span it: the relations $x^2=-xy-y^2$ and $x^3=0$, together with $xy^2=-x^2y$ and $y^3=0$, reduce every monomial of degree $\ge 2$ in $x$ to one of them, and their independence follows by monic division by $y^2+xy+x^2$ over $\mathbb R[x]/(x^3)$, which gives the free basis $1,y$ over that ring. [given, F2]

2.1 **The trace and pairing.** The rank-two summand map $j(p\otimes q)=p\otimes1\otimes1\otimes q$ pulls the Bott–Samelson trace back to $\partial_1\partial_2\partial_1(p)q$, as follows by taking the right-coefficient trace successively in the three slots; this is the explicit trace calculation in the rank-two decomposition proof, also obtained directly from the rank-one trace convention. After right reduction it is the top trace on $C$, since $\partial_1(x_1^2x_2)=x_1x_2$, $\partial_2(x_1x_2)=x_1$ and $\partial_1(x_1)=1$. Hence $\operatorname{Tr}(x^2y)=1$ and all degrees other than $6$ have zero trace. The complementary-degree pairings are $1$ in degrees $0,6$ and $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ in degrees $2,4$, of determinant $-1$; they prove nondegeneracy directly. The form used below is therefore the actual induced reduced intersection form, without invoking the general Hodge theorem. [step 1.1, given, F2, algebra]

3.1 **The special dominant element.** For $\rho=2x+y$ one computes $\rho x=2x^2+xy$ and $\rho y=2xy+y^2=-x^2+xy$ using $y^2=-x^2-xy$; the matrix of $\rho$ from the degree-$2$ block with basis $(x,y)$ to the degree-$4$ block with basis $(x^2,xy)$ is therefore $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is $3\ne0$, so $\rho:C^{-1}\to C^{1}$ is an isomorphism. Moreover $\rho^2x=3x^2y$ and $\rho^2y=0$: indeed $x^2\rho=x^2(2x+y)=2x^3+x^2y=x^2y$, $xy\rho=xy(2x+y)=2x^2y+xy^2=x^2y$; hence $\rho^2x=2\cdot x^2y+x^2y=3x^2y$ and $\rho^2y=-x^2y+x^2y=0$; hence $P^{-1}=\ker(\rho^2)=\mathbb Ry$ and $\rho^3(1)=\rho^2(2x+y)=6x^2y\ne0$, so $\rho^3:C^{-3}\to C^{3}$ is an isomorphism as both sides are one-dimensional. [step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 **The signs for the special element.** With the normalization $\operatorname{Tr}(x^2y)=1$, the bottom primitive form is $(1,1)=\operatorname{Tr}(1\cdot\rho^3(1))=\operatorname{Tr}(6x^2y)=6>0$, positive as required in degree $-3$; the middle primitive form is $(y,y)=\operatorname{Tr}(y\cdot\rho y)=\operatorname{Tr}(y(-x^2+xy))=\operatorname{Tr}(-x^2y+xy^2)=-1-1=-2<0$, negative as required in degree $-1$, where the standard sign is $(-1)^{(3-1)/2}=-1$. The primitive decomposition is read off from the two strings: $1\mapsto 2x+y\mapsto 3x^2+3xy\mapsto 6x^2y$ spans the four degrees with one vector each, and $y\mapsto -x^2+xy$ spans degrees $-1$ and $+1$; together they account for all four graded pieces and their dimensions, so there are exactly one length-four string and one length-two string. [step 3.1, F1]

5.1 **The general dominant chamber.** Let $\rho=c_1x_1+c_2x_2+c_3x_3$ be strictly dominant, so $c_1>c_2>c_3$; subtracting a multiple of $e_1$ (which is zero in $C$) writes its class as $\rho=ax+by$ with $a=c_1-c_3>b=c_2-c_3>0$. Then $\rho x=ax^2+bxy$ and $\rho y=-bx^2+(a-b)xy$, so the middle matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}a&-b\\b&a-b\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $D=a^2-ab+b^2>0$, and $\rho^3(1)=3ab(a-b)x^2y$: indeed $\rho^2x=b(2a-b)x^2y$ and $\rho^2y=a(a-2b)x^2y$, so $p:=a(a-2b)x-b(2a-b)y$ satisfies $\rho^2p=0$, and expanding gives $\operatorname{Tr}(p\rho p)=A^2b-B^2a+2AB(b-a)$ with $A=a(a-2b)$, $B=b(2a-b)$, which simplifies to $-3ab(a-b)(a^2-ab+b^2)<0$. Hence $P^{-1}=\mathbb Rp$ (one-dimensional, since $p\ne0$ for $a>b>0$) carries a negative definite Lefschetz form, the bottom form $\operatorname{Tr}(3ab(a-b)x^2y)>0$ is positive, and every strictly dominant $\rho$ satisfies hard Lefschetz with the standard signs on both primitive spaces. [step 4.1, F1]

6.1 **Conclusion.** Steps 2.1 and 3.1 verify the displayed isomorphisms, the two primitive spaces and their signs for the explicit choice, and step 5.1 shows the same for every strictly dominant element; the primitive decomposition has the two strings claimed. This verifies the example by its quotient and trace calculations. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F1] ∎

2.1 **The trace and pairing.** The rank-two summand map $j(p\otimes q)=p\otimes1\otimes1\otimes q$ pulls the Bott–Samelson trace back to $\partial_1\partial_2\partial_1(p)q$, as follows by taking the right-coefficient trace successively in the three slots; this is the explicit trace calculation in the rank-two decomposition proof, also obtained directly from the rank-one trace convention. After right reduction it is the top trace on $C$, since $\partial_1(x_1^2x_2)=x_1x_2$, $\partial_2(x_1x_2)=x_1$ and $\partial_1(x_1)=1$. Hence $\operatorname{Tr}(x^2y)=1$ and all degrees other than $6$ have zero trace. The complementary-degree pairings are $1$ in degrees $0,6$ and $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ in degrees $2,4$, of determinant $-1$; they prove nondegeneracy directly. The form used below is therefore the actual induced reduced intersection form, without invoking the general Hodge theorem. [step 1.1, given, F2, algebra]

3.1 **The special dominant element.** For $\rho=2x+y$ one computes $\rho x=2x^2+xy$ and $\rho y=2xy+y^2=-x^2+xy$ using $y^2=-x^2-xy$; the matrix of $\rho$ from the degree-$2$ block with basis $(x,y)$ to the degree-$4$ block with basis $(x^2,xy)$ is therefore $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is $3\ne0$, so $\rho:C^{-1}\to C^{1}$ is an isomorphism. 4.1 **The signs for the special element.** With the normalization $\operatorname{Tr}(x^2y)=1$, the bottom primitive form is $(1,1)=\operatorname{Tr}(1\cdot\rho^3(1))=\operatorname{Tr}(6x^2y)=6>0$, positive as required in degree $-3$; the middle primitive form is $(y,y)=\operatorname{Tr}(y\cdot\rho y)=\operatorname{Tr}(y(-x^2+xy))=\operatorname{Tr}(-x^2y+xy^2)=-1-1=-2<0$, negative as required in degree $-1$, where the standard sign is $(-1)^{(3-1)/2}=-1$. [step 3.1, F1]

5.1 **The general dominant chamber.** Let $\rho=c_1x_1+c_2x_2+c_3x_3$ be strictly dominant, so $c_1>c_2>c_3$; subtracting a multiple of $e_1$ (which is zero in $C$) writes its class as $\rho=ax+by$ with $a=c_1-c_3>b=c_2-c_3>0$. Then $\rho x=ax^2+bxy$ and $\rho y=-bx^2+(a-b)xy$, so the middle matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}a&-b\\b&a-b\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $D=a^2-ab+b^2>0$, and $\rho^3(1)=3ab(a-b)x^2y$: indeed $\rho^2x=b(2a-b)x^2y$ and $\rho^2y=a(a-2b)x^2y$, so $p:=a(a-2b)x-b(2a-b)y$ satisfies $\rho^2p=0$, and expanding gives $\operatorname{Tr}(p\rho p)=A^2b-B^2a+2AB(b-a)$ with $A=a(a-2b)$, $B=b(2a-b)$, which simplifies to $-3ab(a-b)(a^2-ab+b^2)<0$. Hence $P^{-1}=\mathbb Rp$ (one-dimensional, since $p\ne0$ for $a>b>0$) carries a negative definite Lefschetz form, the bottom form $\operatorname{Tr}(3ab(a-b)x^2y)>0$ is positive, and every strictly dominant $\rho$ satisfies hard Lefschetz with the standard signs on both primitive spaces. [step 4.1, F1]

6.1 **Conclusion.** Steps 2.1 and 3.1 verify the displayed isomorphisms, the two primitive spaces and their signs for the explicit choice, and step 5.1 shows the same for every strictly dominant element; the primitive decomposition has the two strings claimed. This verifies the example by its quotient and trace calculations. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F1] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Example

Take $n=3$ and let $w_0=s_1s_2s_1$ be the longest element of $S_3$. Then $B_{w_0}=S\otimes_{S^{S_3}}S(3)$ and its reduced module is $C(3)$, where $C=S/(S^{S_3}_+)$ is the unshifted coinvariant algebra: $C$ has the Poincare polynomial $1+2t^2+2t^4+t^6$, so $\dim C=6$, and in the centered grading
$$\dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{-3}=\dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{3}=1,\qquad \dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{-1}=\dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{1}=2 .$$
The standard-basis expansion of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element is
$$\underline H_{w_0}=H_{w_0}+v(H_{s_1s_2}+H_{s_2s_1})+v^2(H_{s_1}+H_{s_2})+v^3,$$
obtained by solving the bar-invariance and triangularity conditions with coefficients in $v^d\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; its coefficients are non-negative, its value at $v=1$ sums to $6=\dim C$, and it agrees with the rank-one and rank-two Kazhdan-Lusztig data $P_{e,w_0}=P_{s_i,w_0}=P_{w,w_0}=1$ for $\ell(w)=2$. Hence $\operatorname{ch}(B_{w_0})=\underline H_{w_0}$: Soergel's conjecture holds for the longest element of $S_3$, and the $\Delta$-multiplicities of the coinvariant bimodule are the six coefficients just displayed, one for each element of $S_3$.
source_proof_sections:
Verification
**Proof technique:** direct; the identification with the invariants-tensor bimodule, an explicit bar-invariance computation in the Hecke algebra, and the comparison of the graded dimensions.

**Given:** $S=\mathbb R[x_1,x_2,x_3]$ with $\deg x_i=2$, the longest element $w_0=s_1s_2s_1$, the rank-two longest bimodule $B_{i,i+1,i}=R\otimes_{R^{W_{i,i+1}}}R(3)$ ([[def-the-rank-two-longest-type-a-soergel-bimodule]]), the reduced module and the character ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]], [[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]), the normalized Hecke algebra with $H_s^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_s$ and the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]), and multiplicativity of the standard character ([[lem-the-type-a-standard-character-is-multiplicative]]).

[F1] The rank-two longest bimodule is $S\otimes_{S^{S_3}}S(3)$ after real scalar extension, and right reduction is tensoring with $S/S_+=\mathbb R$ ([[def-the-rank-two-longest-type-a-soergel-bimodule]], [[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]). The symmetric-polynomial and quotient-basis computations needed here are supplied in step 1.1; no general invariant-ring theorem is assumed.

[F2] In the Hecke algebra $H_s^{-1}=H_s+(v-v^{-1})$ for every simple $s$, and the bar involution acts on the standard basis by $\overline{H_w}=H_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis is the unique basis of elements $\underline H_w=H_w+\sum_{y<w}p_{y,w}H_y$ with $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ and $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]).

[F3] The coefficient of $H_y$ in $\operatorname{ch}(M)$ is $\sum_d(M:\Delta_y(d))v^d$ with non-negative integral multiplicities, and for the standard layer $\Delta_y(d)$ the reduced dimension sits in degree $\ell(y)-d$; hence the multiset of monomials of the character, read with the degrees $\ell(y)-d$, is the graded dimension of the reduced module ([[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]).

[F4] The character is multiplicative with simple value $H_s+v$, and the rank-two decomposition is $B_{s_1}B_{s_2}B_{s_1}\cong B_{w_0}\oplus B_{s_1}$ ([[lem-the-type-a-standard-character-is-multiplicative]], [[thm-rank-two-type-a-soergel-bimodule-decompositions]]).


1.1 **The bimodule and its reduction.** Symmetric polynomials in three variables are generated by $e_1,e_2,e_3$: for a homogeneous symmetric polynomial, its lexicographically leading monomial has exponents $a\ge b\ge c$; subtracting its coefficient times $e_1^{a-b}e_2^{b-c}e_3^c$ lowers that leading monomial. The finite set of monomials of the fixed total degree makes this reduction terminate. Thus $S^{S_3}=\mathbb R[e_1,e_2,e_3]$ and [F1] gives the reduced module $C(3)$ with $C=S/(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Eliminating $x_3=-x-y$ gives $C=\mathbb R[x,y]/(x^3,y^2+xy+x^2)$: the $e_3$ relation is $x^2y+xy^2=0$, and subtracting this from $x(x^2+xy+y^2)=0$ gives $x^3=0$, with the same identities proving the reverse inclusion of ideals. Over $\mathbb R[x]/(x^3)$, division by the monic quadratic in $y$ gives the free basis $1,y$; hence $1,x,y,x^2,xy,x^2y$ is a real basis and the dimensions are $1,2,2,1$ in degrees $0,2,4,6$, centered at $-3,-1,1,3$ after shifting by $(3)$. The tensor bimodule is generated as a bimodule by $1\otimes1$ and its bottom component is one dimensional, so every degree-zero endomorphism is scalar; it is therefore indecomposable. The balanced surjection $f\otimes g\mapsto f w_0(g)$ onto $S_{w_0}$ proves that it has the $w_0$ graph in its support. In the rank-two decomposition it is the summand carrying the $w_0$ graph (the other summand $B_{s_1}$ has only the $e,s_1$ graphs), so its label is $w_0$. [given, F1]

1.2 **The Kazhdan-Lusztig element.** Put $A:=v-v^{-1}$ and $J:=H_{w_0}+v(H_{s_1s_2}+H_{s_2s_1})+v^2(H_{s_1}+H_{s_2})+v^3$. The element $J$ lies in $H_{w_0}+\sum_{y<w_0}v\mathbb Z[v]H_y$, since all coefficients belong to $v\mathbb Z[v]$. For bar-invariance we expand: from $H_s^{-1}=H_s+A$ and the reduced products $H_{s_1}H_{s_2}=H_{s_1s_2}$ and $H_{s_1s_2}H_{s_1}=H_{w_0}$ one computes $\overline{H_{s_1s_2}}=H_{s_1s_2}+A(H_{s_1}+H_{s_2})+A^2$ and $\overline{H_{w_0}}=H_{w_0}+A(H_{s_1s_2}+H_{s_2s_1})+A^2(H_{s_1}+H_{s_2})+A+A^3$, while $\overline{H_{s_1}}=H_{s_1}+A$ and $\overline{H_{s_2}}=H_{s_2}+A$. Applying the semilinear involution to $J$ gives $\overline J=\overline{H_{w_0}}+v^{-1}(\overline{H_{s_1s_2}}+\overline{H_{s_2s_1}})+v^{-2}(\overline{H_{s_1}}+\overline{H_{s_2}})+v^{-3}$; collecting coefficients in the standard basis, the coefficient of $H_{s_1s_2}+H_{s_2s_1}$ becomes $A+v^{-1}=v$, the coefficient of $H_{s_1}+H_{s_2}$ becomes $A^2+2v^{-1}A+v^{-2}=v^2$, and the coefficient of $H_e$ becomes $A+A^3+2v^{-1}A^2+2v^{-2}A+v^{-3}=v^3$. Hence $\overline J=J$, and by the uniqueness clause of [F2] $J=\underline H_{w_0}$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 **Character and multiplicities.** By [F4], $\operatorname{ch}(B_{w_0})=(H_{s_1}+v)(H_{s_2}+v)(H_{s_1}+v)-(H_{s_1}+v)=J$, the last equality following by the quadratic relation $H_s^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_s$ and reduced multiplication. Step 1.2 gives $J=\underline H_{w_0}$, so the $\Delta$-multiplicities of $B_{w_0}$ are exactly the six coefficients of $J$, one for each of the six elements of $S_3$. Reading them through [F3], the layer $\Delta_{w_0}(0)$ contributes in degree $\ell(w_0)=3$, the two layers $\Delta_{s_1s_2}(1),\Delta_{s_2s_1}(1)$ contribute in degree $1$ with multiplicity two, the two layers $\Delta_{s_1}(2),\Delta_{s_2}(2)$ contribute in degree $-1$ with multiplicity two and the layer $\Delta_e(3)$ contributes in degree $-3$; this is the graded dimension $1,2,2,1$ of the centered coinvariant algebra computed in step 1.1, and the value at $v=1$ is $6=\dim C$. The coefficients $P_{e,w_0}=P_{s_i,w_0}=P_{s_1s_2,w_0}=P_{s_2s_1,w_0}=1$ are the classical normalization of these coefficients. This verifies the example. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F3, F4] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Example

Take $n=2$, so $S_n=\{e,s\}$ and $B_s=B_s^R=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$ with $S=\mathbb R[x_1,x_2]$, $\deg x_i=2$ and $\alpha_s=x_1-x_2$. In the right $S$-basis $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ of degrees $-1$ and $+1$ the multiplication relations are
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s .$$
The trace is $\operatorname{Tr}(c_{\mathrm{id}}a+c_sb)=b$ for $a,b\in S$ and the intersection form has the Gram matrix
$$\begin{pmatrix}\langle c_{\mathrm{id}},c_{\mathrm{id}}\rangle&\langle c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\rangle\\ \langle c_s,c_{\mathrm{id}}\rangle&\langle c_s,c_s\rangle\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&\alpha_s\end{pmatrix},$$
whose determinant is $-1$, so the form is non-degenerate, and the induced form on the reduced module is non-degenerate too. The reduced module has the real basis $(\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}},\overline{c_s})$ with degrees $-1$ and $+1$, so $\dim(\overline{B_s})^{-1}=\dim(\overline{B_s})^{1}=1$; for $\rho=\alpha_s/2=(x_1-x_2)/2$, which is strictly dominant with $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)=1$, one computes $\rho\cdot\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}=\overline{c_s}$ and $\rho\cdot\overline{c_s}=0$. Hence $\rho:(\overline{B_s})^{-1}\to(\overline{B_s})^{1}$ is an isomorphism, hard Lefschetz holds, the primitive subspace in degree $-1$ is all of $(\overline{B_s})^{-1}$, and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)=\langle a,\rho b\rangle$ is positive on it: $\langle\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}},\overline{c_s}\rangle=1>0$, matching the Hodge-Riemann sign $(-1)^{(\ell(s)-1)/2}=+1$. Finally $\operatorname{ch}(B_s)=H_s+v=\underline H_s$, the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element of the simple reflection, which is Soergel's conjecture at $s$, and the rational model over $\mathbb Q$ gives the same numbers.
source_proof_sections:

source_claim_sections:
Example

Take $n=2$, so $S_n=\{e,s\}$ and $B_s=B_s^R=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$ with $S=\mathbb R[x_1,x_2]$, $\deg x_i=2$ and $\alpha_s=x_1-x_2$. In the right $S$-basis $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ of degrees $-1$ and $+1$ the multiplication relations are
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s .$$
The trace is $\operatorname{Tr}(c_{\mathrm{id}}a+c_sb)=b$ for $a,b\in S$ and the intersection form has the Gram matrix
$$\begin{pmatrix}\langle c_{\mathrm{id}},c_{\mathrm{id}}\rangle&\langle c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\rangle\\ \langle c_s,c_{\mathrm{id}}\rangle&\langle c_s,c_s\rangle\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&\alpha_s\end{pmatrix},$$
whose determinant is $-1$, so the form is non-degenerate, and the induced form on the reduced module is non-degenerate too. The reduced module has the real basis $(\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}},\overline{c_s})$ with degrees $-1$ and $+1$, so $\dim(\overline{B_s})^{-1}=\dim(\overline{B_s})^{1}=1$; for $\rho=\alpha_s/2=(x_1-x_2)/2$, which is strictly dominant with $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)=1$, one computes $\rho\cdot\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}}=\overline{c_s}$ and $\rho\cdot\overline{c_s}=0$. Hence $\rho:(\overline{B_s})^{-1}\to(\overline{B_s})^{1}$ is an isomorphism, hard Lefschetz holds, the primitive subspace in degree $-1$ is all of $(\overline{B_s})^{-1}$, and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)=\langle a,\rho b\rangle$ is positive on it: $\langle\overline{c_{\mathrm{id}}},\overline{c_s}\rangle=1>0$, matching the Hodge-Riemann sign $(-1)^{(\ell(s)-1)/2}=+1$. Finally $\operatorname{ch}(B_s)=H_s+v=\underline H_s$, the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element of the simple reflection, which is Soergel's conjecture at $s$, and the rational model over $\mathbb Q$ gives the same numbers.

source_claim_sections:
Example

Take $n=3$ and the two simple reflections $s=s_1$, $t=s_2$. The rank-two Bott-Samelson bimodule $B_sB_t$ has character
$$\operatorname{ch}(B_sB_t)=\operatorname{ch}(B_s)\operatorname{ch}(B_t)=(H_s+v)(H_t+v)=H_{st}+vH_s+vH_t+v^2$$
in the standard basis, so its $\Delta$-multiplicities are $1$ at $H_{st}$, $1$ at $H_s$ and at $H_t$ with shift $v$, and $1$ at the identity with shift $v^2$; in particular all multiplicities are non-negative and $\dim(\overline{B_sB_t})=1+1+1+1=4$. In $S_3$ the product $st$ has length $2$ and $B_{st}$ has the same character $\underline H_{st}=H_{st}+vH_s+vH_t+v^2$, so $B_sB_t=B_{st}$ is already indecomposable; equivalently the only summand is the top one $B_{st}$ and all multiplicities $m_y$ for $y<st$ vanish. Similarly $B_sB_tB_s=B_{sts}\oplus B_s$ with characters $\underline H_{sts}+\underline H_s$, whereas $B_tB_sB_t=B_{sts}\oplus B_t$; the two Bott-Samelson products are not isomorphic; the example also verifies the rank-two values of the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials $P_{e,st}=P_{s,st}=P_{t,st}=1$ used on the companion page.
source_proof_sections:
Verification

**Proof technique:** direct; multiplicativity of the character, the explicit two-letter Hecke computation, and comparison with the rank-two decomposition.

**Given:** The simple reflections $s=s_1$, $t=s_2$ of $S_3$, the one-letter bimodules $B_s,B_t$ and the Bott-Samelson product $B_sB_t$ ([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]], [[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]]), the character with its $\Delta$-multiplicities ([[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], [[lem-the-type-a-standard-character-is-multiplicative]]), the normalized Hecke algebra with its two bases and $\underline H_s=H_s+v$ ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]), the rank-two decomposition theorem ([[thm-rank-two-type-a-soergel-bimodule-decompositions]]).

[F1] The character is multiplicative and satisfies $\operatorname{ch}(B_{s_i})=H_{s_i}+v$; the coefficient of $H_y$ in $\operatorname{ch}(M)$ is $\sum_d(M:\Delta_y(d))v^d$, and the reduced dimension of a layer $\Delta_y(d)$ is one in degree $\ell(y)-d$ ([[lem-the-type-a-standard-character-is-multiplicative]], [[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]).

[F2] The standard basis of the Hecke algebra multiplies by $H_uH_s=H_{us}$ when $\ell(us)=\ell(u)+1$; the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis is the unique basis $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]H_y$ of bar-invariant elements ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]).

[F3] The rank-two decomposition theorem: $B_sB_tB_s\cong B_{sts}\oplus B_s$ with no shifts; exchanging $s$ and $t$ gives $B_tB_sB_t\cong B_{sts}\oplus B_t$ ([[thm-rank-two-type-a-soergel-bimodule-decompositions]]).

[F4] The polynomial ring has only nonnegative degrees and degree-zero part $\mathbb R$. The generator has left basis $1\otimes1,1\otimes x_i$ for $s_i$, since $S=S^{s_i}\oplus x_iS^{s_i}$; tensor products have the corresponding finite left bases ([[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]]).

1.1 **The character of the two-letter product.** By [F1] and multiplicativity, $\operatorname{ch}(B_sB_t)=(H_s+v)(H_t+v)=H_sH_t+vH_s+vH_t+v^2$; since $st$ is reduced, [F2] gives $H_sH_t=H_{st}$, so the standard-basis expansion is $H_{st}+vH_s+vH_t+v^2$. Its coefficients give the multiplicities $1,1,1,1$ displayed, and reading the layers through [F1] the reduced dimension is $1+1+1+1=4$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 **The Kazhdan-Lusztig element of $st$.** Put $A:=v-v^{-1}$ and $J:=H_{st}+v(H_s+H_t)+v^2$; then $J\in H_{st}+v\mathbb Z[v]H_s+v\mathbb Z[v]H_t+v^2\mathbb Z[v]$. Since $H_s^{-1}=H_s+A$, $H_t^{-1}=H_t+A$ and $\overline{H_{st}}=H_{ts}^{-1}=H_s^{-1}H_t^{-1}=(H_s+A)(H_t+A)=H_{st}+A(H_s+H_t)+A^2$ (the last identity uses $H_sH_t=H_{st}$), applying the semilinear involution gives $\overline J=\overline{H_{st}}+v^{-1}(\overline{H_s}+\overline{H_t})+v^{-2}=H_{st}+A(H_s+H_t)+A^2+v^{-1}(H_s+H_t)+2v^{-1}A+v^{-2}$, whose coefficients are $A+v^{-1}=v$ at $H_s+H_t$ and $A^2+2v^{-1}A+v^{-2}=(v^2-2+v^{-2})+(2-2v^{-2})+v^{-2}=v^2$ at $H_e$; hence $\overline J=J$, and by uniqueness [F2], $J=\underline H_{st}$. [step 1.1, F2]

3.1 **Indecomposability of $B_sB_t$.** The unshifted tensor $M=S\otimes_{S^s}S\otimes_{S^t}S$ is generated as a bimodule by $1\otimes1\otimes1$. To see this, write a middle polynomial as $h_0+x_1h_1$ with $h_0,h_1\in S^s$, which slide to the first slot. The remaining $x_1$ slides to the last slot because $t=s_2$ fixes $x_1$. Therefore every tensor is a sum of $p(1\otimes1\otimes1)q$. After the shift $(2)$ its lowest component is one-dimensional in degree $-2$, by its finite left tensor basis and $S_0=\mathbb R$. A degree-zero bimodule endomorphism must send the generator to a scalar multiple of itself, and generation forces that same scalar on all of $M$. Hence its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, with no nontrivial idempotent, so $B_sB_t$ is indecomposable. The balanced map $p\otimes q\otimes r\mapsto p\,s(q)\,st(r)$ is surjective onto the $st$ graph bimodule, showing that this indecomposable has the top graph of its reduced word; it is the normalized summand $B_{st}$. Thus $B_sB_t\cong B_{st}$ with no lower summands, independently of the Hom formula. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F4, algebra]

4.1 **The three-letter braid relation.** By multiplicativity and the products computed in steps 1.1 and 2.1, $\operatorname{ch}(B_sB_tB_s)=\underline H_s\underline H_t\underline H_s=\underline H_{st}\underline H_s$; expanding with the Hecke relations gives $\underline H_{st}\underline H_s=\underline H_{sts}+\underline H_s$ Indeed the expansion is $J_0+H_s+v$ where $J_0=H_{sts}+v(H_{st}+H_{ts})+v^2(H_s+H_t)+v^3$. The element $J_0=\underline H_{st}\underline H_s-\underline H_s$ is bar fixed, with triangular lower coefficients in $v\mathbb Z[v]$, so uniqueness in [F2] identifies it with $\underline H_{sts}$. The reduced dimensions add to $6+2=8$. Exchanging $s$ and $t$ in [F3] gives $B_tB_sB_t\cong B_{sts}\oplus B_t$, whose character differs by $\underline H_t-\underline H_s=H_t-H_s\ne0$, so these Bott-Samelson products are not isomorphic; the rank-two Kazhdan-Lusztig data $P_{e,st}=P_{s,st}=P_{t,st}=1$ are the coefficients displayed in step 2.1. This verifies the example. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F3] ∎

To see this, write a middle polynomial as $h_0+x_1h_1$ with $h_0,h_1\in S^s$, which slide to the first slot. The remaining $x_1$ slides to the last slot because $t=s_2$ fixes $x_1$. A degree-zero bimodule endomorphism must send the generator to a scalar multiple of itself, and generation forces that same scalar on all of $M$. Hence its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, with no nontrivial idempotent, so $B_sB_t$ is indecomposable. Proof

**Proof technique:** induction on the length in the standard basis; the ambient algebra is finite free over $A$.

1.1 **Well-definedness and bilinearity (1), (2).** Since $\{H_w\}$ is an $A$-basis by [F1], prescribing $\varepsilon(H_w)=\delta_{e,w}$ and extending $A$-linearly is well defined and unique; the reversal map $a$ is a well-defined $A$-linear anti-automorphism by [F2], and multiplication is $A$-bilinear, so $(h,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ is a well-defined $A$-bilinear form, for $(ph,qh')=\varepsilon(p\,a(h)\,q\,h')=pq\,\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ with $p,q\in A$. This proves (1) and (2). [given, F1, F2]

2.1 **The key identity: base case and recursion.** We prove by induction on $\ell(u)$ that $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$; for $u=e$ this reads $H_eH_y=H_y$ and $\varepsilon(H_y)=\delta_{e,y}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$, and for $u\ne e$ we choose a simple reflection $s$ with $\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$ and note that [F1] applied to $w=us$ gives $H_{us}H_s=H_u$, since $(us)s=u$ has length $\ell(u)=\ell(us)+1$. [base, step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 **The left multiplication rule.** Applying the anti-automorphism $a$ of [F2] to the two cases of [F1] and using $a(H_wH_s)=a(H_s)a(H_w)=H_sH_{w^{-1}}$ and $(ws)^{-1}=sw^{-1}$ gives $H_sH_w=H_{sw}$ if $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)+1$, and $H_sH_w=H_{sw}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w$ if $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$; this is the rule used in the two cases below. [step 2.1, F1, F2]

4.1 **The ascent case.** Keep $u\ne e$ and its right descent $s$ from step 2.1, and let $y\in S_n$ satisfy $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_sH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})$; the induction hypothesis applies to the pair $(us,sy)$, whose first length is $\ell(u)-1$, giving $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,(sy)^{-1}}=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$, and $us=y^{-1}s$ holds if and only if $u=y^{-1}$ (multiply on the right by $s$ and use $s^2=e$), so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$. [step 3.1, ih]

5.1 **The descent case.** Keep $u,s$ as above and let $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}+(v^{-1}-v)H_y$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})+(v^{-1}-v)\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)$; the induction hypothesis gives $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}}$. If $us=y^{-1}$, then $y=(us)^{-1}=su^{-1}$ and, since $us$ is a right descent of $u$, taking inverses gives $\ell(y)=\ell(su^{-1})=\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$, while $\ell(sy)=\ell(u^{-1})=\ell(u)>\ell(y)$, contradicting $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$; hence $\delta_{us,y^{-1}}=0$ and $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$. [step 4.1, ih]

6.1 **The induction concludes.** For every $u\ne e$ the cases $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$ and $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$ exhaust all $y$ for the chosen right descent $s$, and each case reduced the first argument's length; with the base case this proves $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1]

7.1 **Standard orthonormality (4).** For all $x,y$, using $a(H_x)=H_{x^{-1}}$ from [F2] and step 6.1 with $u=x^{-1}$, we get $(H_x,H_y)=\varepsilon(a(H_x)H_y)=\varepsilon(H_{x^{-1}}H_y)=\delta_{x^{-1},y^{-1}}=\delta_{x,y}$, the last equality being injectivity of $w\mapsto w^{-1}$; this proves (4). [step 6.1, F2]

7.2 **The generator trace identity.** By step 6.1, for every $w$ and simple reflection $s$ one has $\varepsilon(H_wH_s)=\delta_{w,s^{-1}}=\delta_{w,s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_sH_w)=\delta_{s,w^{-1}}=\delta_{w,s}$. Extending over the standard basis gives $\varepsilon(zH_s)=\varepsilon(H_sz)$ for every $z\in H$. In particular the common value for $w=s$ is $1$. [step 6.1, F1, algebra]

8.1 **$\varepsilon$ is a trace and yields the adjunctions (3).** Every element of $H$ is a finite $A$-linear combination of words in the generators, and moving each letter of a word for the second factor to the front one at a time with step 7.2 and bilinearity shows $\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(yx)$ for all $x,y\in H$; consequently, for simple $s$ and $h,h'\in H$, using $a(H_s)=H_s$ from [F2], $(hH_s,h')=\varepsilon(a(hH_s)h')=\varepsilon(H_sa(h)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h'H_s)=(h,h'H_s)$ and $(H_sh,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)a(H_s)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)H_sh')=(h,H_sh')$, which proves (3) and shows both left and right multiplication by $H_s$ are self-adjoint for $(-,-)$. [step 7.2, F2, algebra]

8.2 **Values on the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis (5).** Write $\underline H_x=\sum_{u\le x}h_{u,x}H_u$ with $h_{u,x}=p_{u,x}\in\mathbb Z[v]$, $h_{x,x}=1$ and $h_{u,x}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $u<x$, all other coefficients zero, as in [F3]; then bilinearity (2) and orthonormality from step 7.1 give $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)=\sum_uh_{u,x}h_{u,y}$. [step 7.1, F3, algebra]

All six clauses are proved over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$, using only existence and triangularity of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis and no positivity and no choice. [step 8.1, step 8.2, F3, F4, discharge-induction: step 5.1] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Statement

Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $k=\mathbb R$, the bimodule Soergel category has unique finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions. For every $x\in S_n$ there is a unique normalized indecomposable $B_x$ supported on $\{y:y\le x\}$ with top $\Delta$ layer exactly $\Delta_x=R_x(-\ell(x))$. It is the unique summand with the $x$ graph of any reduced Bott-Samelson word for $x$. Every indecomposable is exactly one $B_x(d)$. Its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local, with residue field $k$ under restriction to its rank-one top layer. No Kazhdan-Lusztig character identity is assumed.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

1.1 A finite-dimensional endomorphism algebra and the absence of nontrivial idempotents imply locality. Indeed for an endomorphism $f$ its polynomial minimal relation splits into a power of $T$ and a factor coprime to $T$. The polynomial Chinese remainder identity produces an idempotent separating the nilpotent and invertible parts; indecomposability forces one part to vanish. Thus every $f$ is invertible or nilpotent, and a nonunit $f$ has $1-f$ invertible. Nonunits form a two-sided ideal: multiplication cannot make a nonunit invertible in a finite-dimensional algebra; if two nonunits summed to a unit, dividing their sum would express $1$ as two nonunits, contradicting the invertibility of $1-f$. This is the unique maximal ideal. Its powers eventually vanish: if a power stabilizes, take a minimal finite generating list for that stable ideal and express its last generator using coefficients in the maximal ideal; the invertibility of $1-a$ for such a coefficient eliminates that generator, a contradiction. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Split idempotents until indecomposable summands remain. Each split reduces the positive right rank of its summand, so there are only finitely many splits. The resulting summands have local endomorphism rings by step 1.1. Decompositions are unique: in two finite decompositions, express the identity of one indecomposable as the sum of its composites through the summands of the other. The local maximal ideal cannot contain every composite; an invertible composite gives a split inclusion into one indecomposable summand, hence an isomorphism to it. Remove the common summand and repeat. This proves finite Krull-Schmidt existence and uniqueness. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Decompose a reduced word for $x$. Its top layer is a single $\Delta_x$ by [F4], and the top-layer functor is additive by [F2]. Exactly one indecomposable summand therefore has this graph, with precisely this normalized layer; call it $B_x$. All other summands have support strictly below $x$. This constructs a normalized candidate without any character conjecture. [F2, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Let $M$ be any nonzero Soergel object and choose a maximal support label $x$. The two graph layers $\Gamma_xM$ and $\Gamma^xM$ are identified by multiplication by $p_x$ as in [F2]. Choose one homogeneous basis element $m$ of the latter, and let $d$ make its degree equal to the generator degree of $\Gamma^xB_x(d)$. Choose graph maps $f_0:\Gamma^xB_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$ taking that generator to $m$, and $g_0:\Gamma_xM\to\Gamma_xB_x(d)$ which takes the corresponding element $p_xm$ to the generator $p_xb$ and kills the other basis elements. These maps are homogeneous of degree zero and satisfy the identity on the rank-one $x$ layer. [F2, step 3.1, choose]

5.1 Lift these maps to bimodule maps $f:B_x(d)\to M$ and $g:M\to B_x(d)$. The quotient map $M\to\Gamma^xM$ is the last step of a $\nabla$ flag with $x$ last; its kernel is flagged, so [F3] lifts the map $B_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$. The inclusion $\Gamma_xM\to M$ is the first step of a $\Delta$ flag with $x$ first; its quotient is flagged, so [F3] lifts $g_0$ followed by $\Gamma_xB_x(d)\to B_x(d)$. The first lifted map on the quotient and the second on the submodule agree with the prescribed graph maps. The image identity $\Gamma_xM=\Gamma^xM p_x$ makes their composite $gf$ act as the identity on $\Gamma_xB_x(d)$. Thus $gf$ is not nilpotent, and is invertible by step 1.1. Rescale $g$ by its inverse to exhibit $B_x(d)$ as a summand of $M$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1]

6.1 If $M$ is indecomposable, step 5.1 gives $M\cong B_x(d)$. If two normalized candidates were obtained from different reduced expressions for $x$, applying that same splitting argument to either candidate makes them isomorphic, because their normalized rank-one top degrees force $d=0$. Distinct labels cannot be isomorphic, by their maximal support; distinct shifts at a fixed label cannot be isomorphic, by their top generator degrees. This proves classification and reduced-word independence. [step 3.1, step 5.1]

7.1 Restriction of degree-zero endomorphisms of $B_x$ to its rank-one top layer is a unital homomorphism onto $k$, since homogeneous scalars act there and its endomorphism ring in degree zero is $k$. Its kernel is a maximal ideal. Locality in step 1.1 makes this the unique maximal ideal, so the residue field is $k$. All selections were from finite supports and finite homogeneous bases, and no choice axiom beyond finite choice is used. The statement follows from steps 2.1, 3.1, 6.1 and this residue calculation. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 6.1] ∎

Nonunits form a two-sided ideal: multiplication cannot make a nonunit invertible in a finite-dimensional algebra; if two nonunits summed to a unit, dividing their sum would express $1$ as two nonunits, contradicting the invertibility of $1-f$. This is the unique maximal ideal. Its powers eventually vanish: if a power stabilizes, take a minimal finite generating list for that stable ideal and express its last generator using coefficients in the maximal ideal; the invertibility of $1-a$ for such a coefficient eliminates that generator, a contradiction. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Split idempotents until indecomposable summands remain. Each split reduces the positive right rank of its summand, so there are only finitely many splits. The resulting summands have local endomorphism rings by step 1.1. Decompositions are unique: in two finite decompositions, express the identity of one indecomposable as the sum of its composites through the summands of the other. The local maximal ideal cannot contain every composite; an invertible composite gives a split inclusion into one indecomposable summand, hence an isomorphism to it. Remove the common summand and repeat. This proves finite Krull-Schmidt existence and uniqueness. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Decompose a reduced word for $x$. Its top layer is a single $\Delta_x$ by [F4], and the top-layer functor is additive by [F2]. Exactly one indecomposable summand therefore has this graph, with precisely this normalized layer; call it $B_x$. All other summands have support strictly below $x$. This constructs a normalized candidate without any character conjecture. [F2, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Let $M$ be any nonzero Soergel object and choose a maximal support label $x$. The two graph layers $\Gamma_xM$ and $\Gamma^xM$ are identified by multiplication by $p_x$ as in [F2]. Choose one homogeneous basis element $m$ of the latter, and let $d$ make its degree equal to the generator degree of $\Gamma^xB_x(d)$. Choose graph maps $f_0:\Gamma^xB_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$ taking that generator to $m$, and $g_0:\Gamma_xM\to\Gamma_xB_x(d)$ which takes the corresponding element $p_xm$ to the generator $p_xb$ and kills the other basis elements. These maps are homogeneous of degree zero and satisfy the identity on the rank-one $x$ layer. [F2, step 3.1, choose]

5.1 Lift these maps to bimodule maps $f:B_x(d)\to M$ and $g:M\to B_x(d)$. The quotient map $M\to\Gamma^xM$ is the last step of a $\nabla$ flag with $x$ last; its kernel is flagged, so [F3] lifts the map $B_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$. The inclusion $\Gamma_xM\to M$ is the first step of a $\Delta$ flag with $x$ first; its quotient is flagged, so [F3] lifts $g_0$ followed by $\Gamma_xB_x(d)\to B_x(d)$. The first lifted map on the quotient and the second on the submodule agree with the prescribed graph maps. The image identity $\Gamma_xM=\Gamma^xM p_x$ makes their composite $gf$ act as the identity on $\Gamma_xB_x(d)$. Thus $gf$ is not nilpotent, and is invertible by step 1.1. Rescale $g$ by its inverse to exhibit $B_x(d)$ as a summand of $M$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1]

6.1 If $M$ is indecomposable, step 5.1 gives $M\cong B_x(d)$. If two normalized candidates were obtained from different reduced expressions for $x$, applying that same splitting argument to either candidate makes them isomorphic, because their normalized rank-one top degrees force $d=0$. Distinct labels cannot be isomorphic, by their maximal support; distinct shifts at a fixed label cannot be isomorphic, by their top generator degrees. This proves classification and reduced-word independence. [step 3.1, step 5.1]

7.1 Restriction of degree-zero endomorphisms of $B_x$ to its rank-one top layer is a unital homomorphism onto $k$, since homogeneous scalars act there and its endomorphism ring in degree zero is $k$. Its kernel is a maximal ideal. Locality in step 1.1 makes this the unique maximal ideal, so the residue field is $k$. All selections were from finite supports and finite homogeneous bases, and no choice axiom beyond finite choice is used. The statement follows from steps 2.1, 3.1, 6.1 and this residue calculation. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 6.1] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Statement

Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$, let $B_x$ be the normalized indecomposable bimodule classified by its top support. With right dual $DM=\operatorname{Hom}_{-R}^{\bullet}(M,R)$, one has $DB_x\cong B_x$. Its right reduction has degrees only in $[-\ell(x),\ell(x)]$, all congruent to $\ell(x)$ modulo two, and the two extremal dimensions are one. Hence its reduced graded dimensions are symmetric. Every Bott-Samelson word has a graded perfect symmetric invariant trace form. These assertions assume neither the Kazhdan-Lusztig character conjecture nor hard Lefschetz.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

1.1 The unit has the perfect multiplication form. If a right-free bimodule $M$ has an invariant form, put $a(b)=b c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $b(b')=b'c_s$ in $MB_s$ and define the induced form by $\langle a(u),a(v)\rangle=\partial_s\langle u,v\rangle$, $\langle a(u),b(v)\rangle=\langle b(u),a(v)\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle$, and $\langle b(u),b(v)\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle\alpha_s$. Extend on a right basis by right bilinearity. The relation of [F2] and the identity $\partial_s(fr)=\partial_s(f)r+s(f)\partial_s(r)$ verify that these formulas agree for arbitrary $u,v$, and that left multiplication is self-adjoint. Symmetry follows from symmetry of the preceding form. If $e_i,e_i^*$ are dual right bases for that form, the pairing between bases $(a(e_i),b(e_i))$ and $(b(e_i^*),a(e_i^*))$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\\alpha_sI&I\end{pmatrix}$, using $\partial_s(1)=0$, and has determinant one. Thus perfection is preserved. Iteration yields a perfect symmetric invariant form on every word, exactly its successive rank-one trace multiplication form. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 For finite right-free modules the graded double-dual evaluation is an isomorphism, so $D$ is an involutive contravariant equivalence and takes indecomposables to indecomposables. The invariant perfect word form of step 1.1 identifies a word with its right dual. Generic graph support is unchanged by this duality: in a right basis left multiplication matrices transpose under $D$, so their simultaneous eigencharacters, and hence the graph labels after passing to the polynomial fraction field, are unchanged. A right-free summand has precisely the support closure of those graph labels. Therefore $DB_x$ is an indecomposable summand with the $x$ graph of the same reduced word. Uniqueness in [F1] identifies it with $B_x$ with no shift. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 A word of length $m$ has a homogeneous right basis given by tensor products of the two basis elements in [F2]; its generator degrees lie between $-m$ and $m$ and have parity $m$. Right reduction preserves a split direct-sum decomposition. Since $B_x$ is an unshifted summand of its reduced word of length $m=\ell(x)$, its reduction has these same bounds and parity. The word's bottom degree is the single $1$-tensor. The balanced evaluation of that word on its top graph, obtained by successively twisting the tensor-slot polynomials by the successive prefix permutations, sends this $1$-tensor to $1$. It factors through the rank-one top quotient, and is an isomorphism onto $R_x(m)$ because both generators have degree $-m$. All other summands have no $x$ support; consequently the projection of the bottom tensor into $B_x$ is nonzero. Its bottom dimension is therefore one. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Right duality reverses the degrees of the finite homogeneous basis after reduction. The unshifted duality $DB_x\cong B_x$ from step 2.1 therefore makes the reduced dimensions symmetric and gives top dimension one from the bottom dimension in step 3.1. The perfect trace forms, duality, degree bounds, parity and extremal dimensions have now all been established locally. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎
