Choose the nonzero maps $i\colon P_e\to P_s$ and $p\colon P_s\to P_e$; under the
Struktursatz [[thm-soergels-struktursatz-full-faithfulness-on-projectives]]
their images in $\operatorname{Hom}_C(\mathbb k,C)=\mathbb k\,i_0$ and
$\operatorname{Hom}_C(C,\mathbb k)=\mathbb k\,p_0$ are the generators
$i_0(1)=x$ and $p_0(a+bx)=a$, and the compositions compute
$p_0i_0=0$ on $\mathbb k$ while $i_0p_0=m_x$, multiplication by $x$ on $C$
(equivalently $pi=0$ and $ip$ is a nonzero square-zero
endomorphism; rank one refers to its image under $V$ on $C$). In particular $\operatorname{End}(P_s)\cong C$ is
recovered as the full two-dimensional endomorphism algebra, and the
full-faithfulness comparison is computed on the four projective Hom spaces
rather than claimed for the whole block.

$s(a)=-a$, the empty-word lift is $B_e=S$ and the rank-one lift is
$$B_s=S\otimes_{\mathbb k[a^2]}S(1)$$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]); their right origin

$-1,1$, and the labels $e^{-1}=e$, $s^{-1}=s$ agree with the dictionary of
[[thm-indecomposable-projectives-correspond-to-indecomposable-soergel-modules]].

$l=r$, with annihilator $(l-r)$
([[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]).

filtration on $V(P)$ is asserted.

Example

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work in $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ with the conventions of
[[def-bgg-category-o]]: $\lambda=0$, $\rho=1$, so the regular standards are
$\Delta_1=M(0)$ and $\Delta_s=M(-2)$ for the two elements of
$W=\{1,s\}$, and the singular wall weight is $\mu=-1$, whose shifted value is
$\mu+\rho=0$. The dominant regular integral block is that of $\lambda=0$
([[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]]), and
the wall-crossing functor is that of
[[def-wall-crossing-functor-and-unit-counit]] built from the two-dimensional
translating module $E=L(1)$ with highest weight $\mu-\lambda=-1$ up to Weyl
conjugacy.

**Onto the wall.** Tensoring the two regular standards with the two-dimensional
module and projecting to the central character of the wall preserves the
unique wall standard: $T_{\mathrm{on}}\Delta_1\cong M(-1)$ and
$T_{\mathrm{on}}\Delta_s\cong M(-1)$, since $\Delta_1$ and $\Delta_s$ differ by
the single simple-root lowering and the tensor filtration retains exactly the
labels of weight $-1$ in the shifted parametrization, as in
[[thm-translation-to-and-from-a-wall-on-standard-modules]].

**Back out of the wall.** The wall block at $\mu=-1$ has a single simple
object $M(-1)=L(-1)$ and is semisimple; hence $M(-1)$ is projective and
injective there, and the exact biadjoint return translation
$T_{\mathrm{out}}$ sends it to a projective object of the regular block whose
Verma flag has the two factors $M(0)$ and $M(-2)$, once each, by
[[thm-translation-to-and-from-a-wall-on-standard-modules]]. By biadjunction, its Hom to $L(-2)$ is one-dimensional, since
$T_{\mathrm{on}}L(-2)=M(-1)$; its Hom to $L(0)$ is zero, since
$L(1)\otimes L(0)=L(1)$ has a different central character from $M(-1)$.
Thus its only simple quotient is $L(-2)$, once, and the projective-cover
decomposition identifies it with $P(-2)$.

**Conclusion.** Both $\theta_s\Delta_1$ and $\theta_s\Delta_s$ are therefore
isomorphic to the same nonsplit two-step extension
$$0\longrightarrow M(0)\longrightarrow P(-2)\longrightarrow M(-2)\longrightarrow 0,$$
with class $[\Delta_1]+[\Delta_s]$ in the Grothendieck group, in agreement with
[[lem-wall-crossing-functors-act-on-standard-modules-by-the-two-step-extension]].
Maximal-weight peeling puts $M(0)$ first in the flag; the extension is
nonsplit because $P(-2)$ is indecomposable as a projective cover. The wall
sits at highest weight $-1$, equivalently at shifted parameter $\mu+\rho=0$;
the regular highest weight $0$ is the dominant maximum of the block;
the antidominant minimum is $-2$.

source_claim_sections:
Example

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice. Work in the regular integral
$\mathfrak{sl}_2$ block with $\lambda=0$, $\rho=1$, so $s\cdot0=-2$ and the
singular wall weight is $\mu=-1$ with $\mu+\rho=0$. The indecomposable
projectives are $P_e=M(0)=\Delta_e$ and $P_s=P(-2)$, whose Verma flag is
$\Delta_e,\Delta_s$ with each standard once
([[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]],
[[lem-wall-crossing-compositions-produce-the-projective-with-the-top-standard-label]]).

Set $\mathbb k=\mathbb C$.

**On the standards.** By
[[lem-wall-crossing-functors-act-on-standard-modules-by-the-two-step-extension]]
the wall-crossing functor $\theta_s$ of
[[def-wall-crossing-functor-and-unit-counit]] satisfies
$\theta_s\Delta_e=\theta_s\Delta_s=P_s$, the nonsplit two-step extension of
$\Delta_s$ by $\Delta_e$: the one-letter reduced word
$w=s$ gives $\theta_s\Delta(\lambda)=P(s\cdot\lambda)$ as its unique new
summand, and the flag computation $\Delta_e+\Delta_s$ shows the summand is the
whole object.

**On the projectives.** Exactness of $\theta_s$
([[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]]) applied
to the flag $0\to\Delta_e\to P_s\to\Delta_s\to0$ shows that $\theta_sP_s$ has
standard flag multiplicities $(\Delta_e,\Delta_s)=(2,2)$. Every projective in
this two-simple block is a direct sum of copies of $P_e$ and $P_s$, whose flag
multiplicities are $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$ by BGG reciprocity
([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]]); writing $\theta_sP_s\cong
P_e^{\oplus a}\oplus P_s^{\oplus b}$, the equations $a+b=2$ and $b=2$ give
$a=0$, $b=2$, so
$$\theta_sP_e\cong P_s,\qquad \theta_sP_s\cong P_s\oplus P_s.$$
In the ordered projective bases $(P_e,P_s)$, with columns indexed by the input,
the matrix of $\theta_s$ is therefore $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$.
On the Soergel side $C=\mathbb k[x]/(x^2)$ with $\deg x=2$, $C^s=\mathbb k$,
$V(P_e)=\mathbb k$ and $V(P_s)=C$; the wall-crossing theorem
[[thm-wall-crossing-under-the-soergel-functor-is-tensoring-with-the-coinvariant-soergel-bimodule]]
gives
$$V\theta_s(P_e)=C\otimes_{C^s}\mathbb k\cong C,\qquad V\theta_s(P_s)=C\otimes_{C^s}C\cong C\oplus C$$
as left $C$-modules, the left $C$-acting on the first factor, and the
projective Struktursatz
[[thm-soergels-struktursatz-full-faithfulness-on-projectives]] reflects these
isomorphisms back to the projective identities above, all objects involved
being projective.

**Dimension comparison.** The tensor $C\otimes_{C^s}C\cong C\otimes_{\mathbb k}C$
is the four-dimensional coinvariant bimodule $=2|W|$ with $|W|=2$, explicitly
spanned by the four elements $1\otimes1,1\otimes x,x\otimes1,x\otimes x$; the
isomorphism $C\oplus C\to C\otimes_{\mathbb k}C$ of left $C$-modules sends
$(u,v)$ to $u\otimes1+v\otimes x$. By contrast the right-reduced polynomial
$B_s=\mathbb k[a]\otimes_{\mathbb k[a^2]}\mathbb k[a](1)$ is only
two-dimensional, with generator degrees $-1,1$ after centering; the right-reduced polynomial module is $C(1)$, whereas the
coinvariant bimodule $C\otimes_{\mathbb k}C$ has dimension four. The former
models $V\theta_s(P_e)$ and the latter the tensor operator applied to
$V(P_s)=C$.

[[thm-wall-crossing-under-the-soergel-functor-is-tensoring-with-the-coinvariant-soergel-bimodule]]

projective Struktursatz
[[thm-soergels-struktursatz-full-faithfulness-on-projectives]] reflects these
isomorphisms back to the projective identities above, all objects involved
being projective.

two-dimensional, with generator degrees $-1,1$ after centering; the right-reduced polynomial module is $C(1)$, whereas the

source_claim_sections:
Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ be dominant regular integral,
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$, $R=S_{(0)}$, and $P_R=P_R(w_0,\lambda)$ the deformed
antidominant projective. Write $\operatorname{HC}_\rho\colon Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to S^W$
for the published shifted Harish-Chandra isomorphism,
$\sigma_\lambda(f)(\epsilon)=f(\lambda+\rho+\epsilon)$, and define
$$a_\lambda\colon Z\otimes_{\mathbb C}R\longrightarrow R\otimes_{R^W}R,\qquad z\otimes r\longmapsto\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))\otimes r.$$
Then $a_\lambda$ and the action map $Z\otimes R\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)$
are surjective and have the same kernel, inducing a canonical $R$-algebra
isomorphism
$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)\cong R\otimes_{R^W}R.$$
On a generic Verma constituent of highest weight $x\cdot\lambda+\epsilon$, $z$
acts by the scalar
$\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z)(x(\lambda+\rho)+\epsilon)=\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))(x^{-1}\epsilon)$;
these scalars vary with $x$, and the center need not act by a single scalar on
$P_R$. After tensoring the right $R$ factor with the residue field at $0$, the
endomorphism algebra becomes $C=S/(S^W_+S)$. More generally, for dot-dominant
integral $\nu$ the corresponding algebra is $R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R$, where
$W_\nu$ is the dot stabilizer. Translation out of that facet identifies the
singular antidominant projective with the regular one; under these shifted
Harish-Chandra identifications, its induced endomorphism map is the inclusion
$R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R\hookrightarrow R\otimes_{R^W}R$.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The block at $\eta=-\rho$ has a single highest weight in $W\cdot\eta\cap(\eta-Q^+)=\{\eta\}$, so $M(\eta)=L(\eta)$ is simple, its projective cover has a Verma flag whose single factor is $L(\eta)$ by BGG reciprocity, hence equals $L(\eta)$ and $L(\eta)$ is projective; with a single simple object and enough projectives the block is semisimple, so $L(\eta)$ is injective as well, and the well-definedness part of [F6] then supplies the object $Q=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\lambda}(E\otimes L(\eta))$, which is projective and injective and has a Verma flag with the factors $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$, $x\in W$, once each, together with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(Q,L(a))\cong\mathbb C$ and a split embedding $P(a)\hookrightarrow Q$; the same construction with the distinct extremal weights $Wv=W/W_\nu$ gives the singular once-each flag. [F1, F6]

1.2 Let $p$ be a height-one prime of $R$, $T=R_p$, $k=\operatorname{Frac}(R/p)$, and let $\tau$ be the tautological parameter of the deformed family; the residual central characters are the $W$-classes of the points $xv+\tau$, $x\in W$, and $\chi_{xv+\tau}=\chi_{yv+\tau}$ over $k$ forces $xv+\tau=w(yv+\tau)$ for some $w$ by [F1] and finite interpolation, so comparing the constant and linear parts modulo $p$ gives $xv=wyv$ and $w\tau=\tau$ in $k$; a nonidentity $w$ fixing the generic point of the divisor $p$ fixes a hyperplane, hence is the orthogonal reflection in that hyperplane. That hyperplane must be a root hyperplane: otherwise it contains a root-regular real point, whose open chamber would be stabilized by $w$, contradicting [[thm-the-weyl-group-acts-simply-transitively-on-weyl-chambers]]. Thus $p$ is the root prime $\langle\tau,\alpha^\vee\rangle$ for that root; therefore at every nonroot prime all residual characters are pairwise distinct, while at the root prime the equal-character classes are exactly the pairs $\{x,s_\alpha x\}$ together with singleton classes wherever $s_\alpha xv=xv$, which occurs in the singular case. [F1, F8, algebra]

1.3 At a root divisor, isolate one two-element residual character class by CRT. Write its upper and lower weights $A=a+\tau$ and $B=b+\tau$, where $b=s_\alpha\cdot a=a-n\alpha$ and $n=\langle a+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle>0$. Over $k=\operatorname{Frac}(R/p)$, a singular vector of weight $A-\gamma$ must satisfy the Casimir equation $2(A+\rho,\gamma)=(\gamma,\gamma)$. Its parameter term vanishes identically on the divisor only if $\gamma$ is a multiple of $\alpha$, and its constant term then forces $\gamma=n\alpha$. The Shapovalov determinant on that weight has valuation one: only its $(\alpha,n)$ factor vanishes, with exponent $K(0)=1$, so its residue radical has dimension one there. A nonzero radical has a highest-weight vector, by choosing minimal root height among its nonzero weight spaces; it is therefore generated initially by that one-dimensional $B$-weight space. The same Casimir equation for $B$ has no solution with positive $\gamma$, so $M(B)$ is simple. Its highest vector gives an injected $M(B)\to M(A)$: the induced map is injective because its simple source is nonzero. Any nonzero quotient of the radical by this image would again have a highest-weight vector; the equation forces weight $B$, but its $B$-space is zero. Thus $\operatorname{Rad}M(A)=M(B)$ and $M(A)$ has length two. This proves the required divisor-field classification directly; no closed-point or complex-only classification is substituted for it. [F2, F3, algebra]

1.4 Let $u=\nu+\rho$ be dominant with $H=\operatorname{Stab}(u)$, and $v=\lambda+\rho$ regular dominant. For onto translation, a retained factor satisfies $yv+\gamma=xu$. The norm bound and dominant-distance inequality force equality $|\gamma|=|u-v|$ and $x^{-1}yv\in Hv$; because $v$ is regular this means $x^{-1}y\in H$, hence $xu=yu$. Thus the retained standard is $\Delta(y\cdot\nu)$ once. This uses the coset condition, not the false assertion $Hv=\{v\}$. For return translation the retained labels are $x\in yH$, each extremal weight once. The conclusion is a Verma flag with factors $\Delta(yh\cdot\lambda)$ for $h\in H$, not a direct sum. The same calculation applies to the deformed tensor flags, with the common parameter $\tau$ retained. [F4, F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 Every standard $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ contains $L(a)$ as a composition factor: $a$ is the minimal weight of $W\cdot a$, so the Verma embedding criterion gives a nonzero, hence injective, map $M(a)=L(a)\to\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$, and BGG reciprocity gives $(P(a):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))=[\Delta(x\cdot\lambda):L(a)]\ge1$, while $(P(a):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))\le(Q:\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))=1$ because $P(a)$ is a summand of $Q$; hence all multiplicities equal one, the complementary summand of $P(a)$ in $Q$ has flag length zero, and $Q=P(a)$; the argument applies verbatim to a dot-dominant singular $\nu$ with $Wv$ replaced by $W/W_\nu$. [F6, step 1.1]

2.2 Put $K=\operatorname{Frac}R$ and $B=R\otimes_{R^W}R$. Localization of the free invariant/harmonic decomposition in [F8] makes it finite free of rank $|W|$ over the right $R$. Evaluation embeds it into $K^W$ by $f\otimes r\mapsto(f(x^{-1}\tau)r)_x$: generically the orbit has $|W|$ distinct points, interpolation makes this map surjective after tensoring with $K$, and freeness makes it injective over $R$. At a nonroot height-one prime, residual orbit points are distinct and CRT gives $B_T=T^W$. At a root prime CRT isolates the pairs from step 1.2. Every pair evaluation is congruent modulo the root uniformizer $\alpha=\langle\tau,\alpha^\vee\rangle$. Choose a linear $f$ for which the two values differ by a unit times $\alpha$; subtract its lower value and multiply by the pair projector to obtain $(\alpha,0)$. Together with the pair identity this generates exactly the congruence order $\{(u,v)\in T^2:u-v\in\alpha T\}$. For a singular stabilizer $H=W_\nu$, Reynolds averaging on the first factor identifies $B^H=R^H\otimes_{R^W}R$. It is finite projective over right $R$ as a split summand of $B$, hence free since $R$ is local; its generic rank is $|W/H|$. The same pair and singleton orders, now on cosets, follow by taking the $H$-fixed tuples. [F8, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Localize $P_R$ to $T=R_p$. Its full flag still has $|W|$ factors; CRT in the finitely many residual central characters splits it into pair components and singleton components. Write $P_{T,\{A,B\}}$ for one pair summand. Only this summand has the two factors $\Delta_T(A)$ and $\Delta_T(B)$ once. Maximal-weight generation gives $0\to\Delta_T(A)\to P_{T,\{A,B\}}\to\Delta_T(B)\to0$. It is projective in its character component by base change and splitting. The residual extension cannot split: otherwise its direct summand $M(B)$ would be projective, but duality applied to the nonsplit length-two $M(A)$ yields a nonsplit extension $0\to L(A)\to D M(A)\to L(B)=M(B)\to0$, contradicting projectivity. At a singleton the summand has a single standard. The identical argument applies to the singular once-each flag, with root-fixed labels giving singletons. Over the fraction field all standard characters are distinct and all Vermas are simple by the Shapovalov determinant; hence each component is its indicated standard and the generic endomorphism algebra is the tuple algebra. [F3, F5, F7, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Translation out carries $P_R^\nu$ to a regular projective by the exact tensor biadjunction and the actual central projectors. Its flag contains every regular standard once by steps 2.1 and 1.4. On the closed fiber, onto translation takes the regular antidominant simple Verma to the singular antidominant simple Verma, so adjunction gives a one-dimensional Hom from the return projective to the regular antidominant simple. Its regular antidominant cover splits off; both have every standard once, so the complement has zero flag and vanishes. Hom base change and the two-map lifting argument of [F7] now give $T_{\mathrm{out}}P_R^\nu\cong P_R^\lambda$. Any two choices induce the same endomorphism map after identification, since the endomorphism algebra is commutative (as will follow from its generic tuple embedding). [F6, F7, step 2.1, step 1.4, algebra]

4.1 Any endomorphism $f$ of the isolated pair $P_{T,\{A,B\}}$ preserves $\Delta_T(A)$ and acts by scalars $u_a$ on $\Delta_T(A)$ and $u_b$ on $\Delta_T(B)$; if $u_a-u_b$ were a unit modulo $p$, the residual projector $(f-u_b)/(u_a-u_b)$, polynomial in $f$ since $(f-u_a)(f-u_b)=0$ on the two-step flag, would split the nonsplit residual extension of step 3.1, so $u_a\equiv u_b$ modulo $\tau(\alpha^\vee)$ and $\operatorname{End}(P_{T,\{A,B\}})$ lies in the congruence order; the central Casimir element acts on the two generic standards by $(A,A+2\rho)$ and $(B,B+2\rho)$, eigenvalues differing by $2n(\alpha,\tau)=n(\alpha,\alpha)\langle\tau,\alpha^\vee\rangle$, a unit times the uniformizer, so the Casimir minus the lower eigenvalue gives the pair $(\tau(\alpha^\vee),0)$ and together with the identity generates the full congruence order, both generators being central actions; on singleton classes the order is $T$, generated by the identity. [F1, F2, step 3.1]

5.1 The generic tuple embeddings place $\operatorname{End}(P_R)$ and $B$ (or $\operatorname{End}(P_R^\nu)$ and $B^H$) inside the same tuple algebra. Both are finite free right-$R$ modules: for End this is [F7], for $B^H$ it is Reynolds averaging in step 2.2. Steps 3.1, 2.2 and 4.1 identify their localizations at each height-one prime, pair by pair, including the singular singletons. A finite free $R$-lattice equals the intersection of its height-one localizations inside its fraction-field span. Indeed $R$ is a localization of a polynomial UFD, and $R=\bigcap_{\operatorname{ht}p=1}R_p$: a reduced fractional denominator outside $R$ has a nonunit irreducible factor detected at its prime; applying this coefficientwise to any free lattice basis proves the lattice assertion. Thus the two lattices are equal and yield the asserted algebra identification. This does not yet assert that the global central image is saturated; its surjectivity is established separately below. [F7, F8, step 2.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 For a dominant shifted weight $u$ with stabilizer $H$, the closed right fiber of $B^H$ is $C^H$, because averaging commutes with quotienting by the right maximal ideal. Choose $N$ above the largest ordinary polynomial degree in $C$, and choose an $H$-invariant representative $h(\tau)$ of any prescribed class in $C^H$ by averaging. Prescribe the jet $h(X-u)$ of order $N$ at $u$, and zero jets at the other distinct points in $Wu$. Polynomial CRT produces $q$ with those jets. Then $p(X)=|H|^{-1}\sum_{w\in W}q(w^{-1}X)$ is $W$-invariant. At $X=u+\tau$, precisely the $w\in H$ terms contribute, and their jets equal $h(w^{-1}\tau)=h(\tau)$; the other terms vanish to order $N$. Hence $p(u+\tau)\equiv h(\tau)\pmod{(\tau)^N}$, whose image in $C$ is the prescribed class. In the regular case take $u=v$ and $H=1$; in the singular case take the actual singular $u$, never regular $v$. By [F1], $p=\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z)$ for a central element $z$. [F1, F8, F9, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 The image of $a_\lambda$ is an $R$-submodule of the finite free target $B$ respectively $B^H$ whose cokernel is finitely generated and has zero closed fiber by step 6.1; Nakayama over the local ring $R$ makes the cokernel zero, so $a_\lambda$ is surjective, and the action map $Z\otimes R\to\operatorname{End}(P_R)$ is surjective with it under the identification of step 5.1. [F7, step 5.1, step 6.1]

8.1 Under the tuple identification, $z\otimes r$ acts on the generic constituent of highest weight $x\cdot\lambda+\tau$ by the scalar $\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z)(x(\lambda+\rho)+\tau)r=\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))(x^{-1}\tau)r$, these scalars vary with $x$, and the injective tuple embedding shows that an element of $Z\otimes R$ acts by zero if and only if its image in $B$ respectively $B^H$ is zero; hence the action map and $a_\lambda$ have the same kernel and induce the displayed isomorphism, while, writing $k=R/\mathfrak m=\mathbb C$ for the residue field (distinct from the coinvariant algebra $C$), tensoring the right factor with $k$ gives $(R\otimes_{R^W}R)\otimes_R k\cong R/(R^W_+R)=C$ respectively $(R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R)\otimes_R k\cong C^{W_\nu}$. [F1, step 5.1, step 7.1]

9.1 On generic constituents translation out repeats the scalar attached to a coset $yH$ on every branch $yh$, so under the identifications of steps 5.1 and 8.1 the map $\operatorname{End}(P_R^\nu)\to\operatorname{End}(T_{\mathrm{out}}P_R^\nu)=\operatorname{End}(P_R^\lambda)$ induced by the translation identification of step 3.2 is the inclusion $R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R\hookrightarrow R\otimes_{R^W}R$; this holds uniformly across the facet, including the regular case $W_\nu=\{1\}$, where it is the identity. [step 3.2, step 5.1, step 8.1] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ be dominant regular integral,
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$, $R=S_{(0)}$, and $P_R=P_R(w_0,\lambda)$ the deformed
antidominant projective. Write $\operatorname{HC}_\rho\colon Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to S^W$
for the published shifted Harish-Chandra isomorphism,
$\sigma_\lambda(f)(\epsilon)=f(\lambda+\rho+\epsilon)$, and define
$$a_\lambda\colon Z\otimes_{\mathbb C}R\longrightarrow R\otimes_{R^W}R,\qquad z\otimes r\longmapsto\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))\otimes r.$$
Then $a_\lambda$ and the action map $Z\otimes R\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)$
are surjective and have the same kernel, inducing a canonical $R$-algebra
isomorphism
$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)\cong R\otimes_{R^W}R.$$
On a generic Verma constituent of highest weight $x\cdot\lambda+\epsilon$, $z$
acts by the scalar
$\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z)(x(\lambda+\rho)+\epsilon)=\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))(x^{-1}\epsilon)$;
these scalars vary with $x$, and the center need not act by a single scalar on
$P_R$. After tensoring the right $R$ factor with the residue field at $0$, the
endomorphism algebra becomes $C=S/(S^W_+S)$. More generally, for dot-dominant
integral $\nu$ the corresponding algebra is $R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R$, where
$W_\nu$ is the dot stabilizer. Translation out of that facet identifies the
singular antidominant projective with the regular one; under these shifted
Harish-Chandra identifications, its induced endomorphism map is the inclusion
$R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R\hookrightarrow R\otimes_{R^W}R$.

source_claim_sections:
Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published invariant-theory
items. Let $W$ act on the Cartan space $\mathfrak h$ by reflections and on
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$ by graded algebra automorphisms, with coinvariant algebra
$C=S/I$ as in [[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]]. Let
$w_1,\dots,w_r$ be homogeneous basic invariants of page degrees
$2d_1,\dots,2d_r$, where $d_1,\dots,d_r$ are the classical degrees
($\deg\mathfrak h=1$; for the Cartan of $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ they are
$2,3,\dots,n$), so that $S^W=\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$
([[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]]), and let
$\rho:S\to C$ be the quotient by the ideal $I=(w_1,\dots,w_r)$. Put
$N:=\sum_{i=1}^r(d_i-1)$. Then:

1. The sequence $w_1,\dots,w_r$ is a homogeneous $S$-regular sequence and $C$
is a complete intersection: $C=S/(w_1,\dots,w_r)$ with
$$\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\frac{\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})}{(1-t^2)^r}=\prod_i(1+t^2+\cdots+t^{2(d_i-1)}),$$
so that $\dim_{\mathbb C}C_{2N}=1$ and $C_j=0$ for $j>2N$.
2. The multiplication pairing $C_i\times C_{2N-i}\to C_{2N}\cong\mathbb C$ is
nondegenerate for every $i$, and consequently
$$\operatorname{soc}(C)=\{c\in C:C_+c=0\}=C_{2N}$$ is one dimensional.
3. Equivalently, $C$ is a graded Gorenstein algebra with one-dimensional socle
in the top degree $2N$.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The invariant ideal is generated by the basic invariants: $I=S\,S^W_+=(w_1,\dots,w_r)$, because $S^W=\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$ and every element of $S^W_+$ is a polynomial in the $w_i$ with zero constant term. Hence $C=S/(w_1,\dots,w_r)$; since $C$ is generated by the images of the degree-two elements, its augmentation ideal satisfies $C_+=(x_1,\dots,x_r)C$. [F1]

1.2 The $r$ basic invariants form an $S$-regular sequence: they are minimal homogeneous invariant generators of $I$ (they generate $I$, and no $w_i$ lies in the ideal generated by the others, since applying the $S^W$-linear Reynolds projection to a relation in $S$ would give a relation in $\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$, where no variable belongs to the ideal generated by the others), and by [F2] the minimal homogeneous invariant generators of $I$ are $r$ in number with common zero set $\{0\}$ and form an $S$-regular sequence; consequently, by [F3], $K(\mathbf w;S)$ is a finite free resolution of $C$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.3 The variables $x_1,\dots,x_r$ form an $S$-regular sequence with $S/(x_1,\dots,x_r)=\mathbb C=:k$, by [F5]; consequently, by [F3], $K(\mathbf x;S)$ is a finite free resolution of $k$. [F3, F5]

1.4 Koszul differentials vanish after base change to $k$: tensoring $K(\mathbf w;S)$ with $k$ multiplies by the images of the $w_i$ in $k$, which lie in the positive-degree part and hence act as zero; so $H_r(K(\mathbf w;S)\otimes_Sk)=K_r(\mathbf w;S)\otimes_Sk$, a one-dimensional space in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i$. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 First computation: by resolution 1.2, resolving the $C$ variable, and the balance isomorphism [F6], $\operatorname{Tor}^S_r(C,k)\cong H_r(K(\mathbf w;S)\otimes_Sk)$, which by step 1.4 is one dimensional and concentrated in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i$. [F3, F6, step 1.2, step 1.4]

2.2 Second computation: by resolution 1.3, resolving the $k$ variable, and [F6], $\operatorname{Tor}^S_r(C,k)\cong H_r(C\otimes_SK(\mathbf x;S))=H_r(K(\mathbf x;C))$; by [F3] the top homology is $\{c\in C:x_ic=0\text{ for all }i\}$, placed in internal degree $2r$ above the degrees of its elements, since $e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_r$ carries degree $2r$. [F3, F6, step 1.3]

2.3 Hilbert series: applying the Euler characteristic to the finite free resolution $K(\mathbf w;S)$ of $C$ gives $$\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})\cdot\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t)=\frac{\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})}{(1-t^2)^r}=\prod_i(1+t^2+\cdots+t^{2(d_i-1)}),$$ the last equality by cancelling one factor $1-t^2$ per invariant. Hence $\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$ is a polynomial of degree $2N$ with leading coefficient $1$, so $\dim_{\mathbb C}C_{2N}=1$ and $C_j=0$ for $j>2N$; the classical formula [F4] gives the same series after substituting $t^2$ for $t$. [F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Comparing steps 2.1 and 2.2 through the natural isomorphism [F6] identifies the top Koszul homology of step 2.2 with a one-dimensional space in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i$; shifting back by the degree $2r$ of the top exterior generator, the space $\{c\in C:x_ic=0\text{ for all }i\}$ is one dimensional and concentrated in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i-2r=2\sum_i(d_i-1)=2N$. [F6, step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 Since $C_+=(x_1,\dots,x_r)C$ by step 1.1, the space of step 3.1 is exactly the socle $\operatorname{soc}(C)=\{c\in C:C_+c=0\}$; it is one dimensional in degree $2N$. The top graded piece $C_{2N}$ is one dimensional by step 2.3, and every element of $C_{2N}$ is annihilated by $C_+$ because $C$ has no degrees above $2N$; hence $0\neq C_{2N}\subseteq\operatorname{soc}(C)$ and both are one dimensional in degree $2N$, so $\operatorname{soc}(C)=C_{2N}$. [step 1.1, step 2.3, step 3.1]

5.1 Nondegeneracy of the top pairing: let $0\neq c\in C_i$ be homogeneous and consider the nonzero graded ideal $cC$ of the finite-dimensional graded algebra $C$; let $m$ be the largest degree with $(cC)_m\neq0$, so $m\le2N$ by step 2.3. Choose $0\neq y\in(cC)_m$; then $C_+y\subseteq(cC)_{>m}=0$, so $y\in\operatorname{soc}(C)=C_{2N}$ by step 4.1, forcing $m=2N$. Writing $y=cb$ with $b\in C_{2N-i}$ gives a nonzero product $cb$, so the pairing $C_i\times C_{2N-i}\to C_{2N}\cong\mathbb C$ has no nonzero left radical; by commutativity it has no nonzero right radical either, and finite-dimensionality of the two sides makes it a perfect pairing for every $i$. Hence $C$ is a graded Gorenstein algebra with one-dimensional socle in top degree $2N$. [step 2.3, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published invariant-theory
items. Let $W$ act on the Cartan space $\mathfrak h$ by reflections and on
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$ by graded algebra automorphisms, with coinvariant algebra
$C=S/I$ as in [[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]]. Then there
is a $W$-stable graded subspace $\mathcal H\subseteq S$, finite dimensional of
dimension $|W|$, such that the multiplication map
$$S^W\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathcal H\longrightarrow S,\qquad p\otimes h\mapsto ph,$$
is an isomorphism of graded $S^W$-modules and of $W$-modules, and the
restriction of the quotient map $\rho:S\to C$ to $\mathcal H$ is an isomorphism
of graded $W$-modules $\mathcal H\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }C$. One may take
$$\mathcal H=\{f\in S:\partial_pf=0\text{ for all }p\in S^W_+\},$$
using constant-coefficient differential operators from a $W$-invariant
positive definite form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$. Any $W$-stable graded
complement of $I$ has the same multiplication and quotient properties. This
is the simultaneous kernel of all positive-degree invariant differential
operators, not in general the kernel of the quadratic Laplacian alone. In particular $\dim\mathcal H_d=\dim C_d$ for every $d$ and
$\sum_d\dim\mathcal H_d=|W|$.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Choose an arbitrary positive definite symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ and average it over the finite group $W$, obtaining a $W$-invariant positive definite form $(\ ,\ )$; choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\dots,e_r$ of $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ for it. On the symmetric algebra $S=\mathbb C[e_1,\dots,e_r]$ let $\langle\ ,\ \rangle$ be the Fischer pairing, the sesquilinear form with $\langle e^{\alpha},e^{\beta}\rangle=\alpha!\,\delta_{\alpha\beta}$ on monomials $e^{\alpha}$ ($\alpha$ a multi-index); it is positive definite, and $W$ acts on $S$ by orthogonal transformations for it because the form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ is $W$-invariant. For $p\in S$ let $\partial_p=p(\partial_1,\dots,\partial_r)$ be substitution of the partial derivatives $\partial_i=\partial/\partial e_i$; then multiplication by $p$ has adjoint $\partial_{\overline p}$, i.e. $\langle pf,g\rangle=\langle f,\partial_{\overline p}g\rangle$, as checked on monomials. Choose real basic invariants: real and imaginary parts of complex invariants are invariant, and one may choose a real homogeneous basis of the indecomposables of the invariant algebra and lift it; its complexification gives basic generators. Complex conjugation preserves $S^W_+$, so simultaneous kernels are unchanged. Set $\mathcal H_d:=I_d^{\perp}$ inside the finite-dimensional space $S_d$, and $\mathcal H:=\bigoplus_d\mathcal H_d$. [F3, construct]

1.2 The invariant ring acts on $S$ with the expected Hilbert series: $S$ has a finite homogeneous $S^W$-basis by [F1], say of degrees $m_1,\dots,m_{|W|}$; their images in $S/S^W_+S=C$ form a $\mathbb C$-basis by graded Nakayama, so $\sum_jt^{m_j}=\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$ and therefore $\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 By step 1.1 the spaces $S_d=I_d\oplus\mathcal H_d$ are orthogonal direct sums and $\mathcal H$ is a graded subspace; it is $W$-stable because $W$ preserves the form and $I$ is a $W$-stable homogeneous ideal, and $\mathcal H$ is a graded complement of $I$. Moreover $\mathcal H_d=\{f\in S_d:\partial_pf=0\text{ for all }p\in S^W_+\}$: since $I=(w_1,\dots,w_r)$, one has $f\in I_d^{\perp}$ exactly when $\langle f,w_ig\rangle=0$ for every $i$ and every $g\in S_{d-2d_i}$, which by adjointness is $\langle\partial_{w_i}f,g\rangle=0$ for all such $g$, hence $\partial_{w_i}f=0$ by positive definiteness; and for $p=\sum_iq_iw_i$ one has $\partial_p=\sum_i\partial_{q_i}\partial_{w_i}$, so vanishing for the $w_i$ is vanishing for all of $S^W_+$. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The restriction $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\to C$ is an isomorphism of graded vector spaces because $\rho$ has kernel $I$ and $\mathcal H$ is a complement of $I$ by step 1.1; it is a map of $W$-modules because $\rho$ is $W$-equivariant. Hence $\dim\mathcal H_d=\dim C_d$ for every $d$, and $\dim\mathcal H=\dim C=|W|$ by [F2]. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $\varphi:S^W\otimes\mathcal H\to S$, $p\otimes h\mapsto ph$. This is a homomorphism of graded $S^W$-modules and of $W$-modules. Its reduction modulo $S^W_+$, namely $\mathcal H\to C$, $h\mapsto\rho(h)$, is surjective because it is the isomorphism $\rho|_{\mathcal H}$ of step 2.2. [step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 The map $\varphi$ is surjective: given homogeneous $f\in S_d$, choose $h\in\mathcal H_d$ with $\rho(f)=\rho(h)$ by step 3.1; then $f-h\in I_d=\sum_i(w_iS)_d=\sum_iw_iS_{d-2d_i}$, so by induction on $d$ each $w_ig$ with $g\in S_{d-2d_i}$ lies in $S^W\cdot\mathcal H$, and adding $h$ exhibits $f$ in the image. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The map $\varphi$ is injective: by steps 1.2 and 2.2 the two sides have the same Hilbert series, $$\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W\otimes\mathcal H,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal H,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t),$$ both are graded with finite-dimensional graded pieces, and by step 4.1 the kernel of the surjective graded $S^W$-linear map $\varphi$ would otherwise contribute positive Hilbert series. Hence $\varphi$ is an isomorphism. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Steps 2.1, 2.2 and 5.1 give a $W$-stable graded complement $\mathcal H$ of $I$ with $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\cong C$ and $S^W\otimes\mathcal H\cong S$; the description of $\mathcal H$ as the simultaneous invariant differential kernel follows from the adjointness $\langle pf,g\rangle=\langle f,\partial_{\overline p}g\rangle$ of step 1.1, and $\dim\mathcal H=|W|$ by step 2.2. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the invariant-theory suppliers [F1] and [F2]; the construction itself uses only finite averages and finite-dimensional linear algebra. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 5.1] ∎

Moreover $\mathcal H_d=\{f\in S_d:\partial_pf=0\text{ for all }p\in S^W_+\}$: since $I=(w_1,\dots,w_r)$, one has $f\in I_d^{\perp}$ exactly when $\langle f,w_ig\rangle=0$ for every $i$ and every $g\in S_{d-2d_i}$, which by adjointness is $\langle\partial_{w_i}f,g\rangle=0$ for all such $g$, hence $\partial_{w_i}f=0$ by positive definiteness; and for $p=\sum_iq_iw_i$ one has $\partial_p=\sum_i\partial_{q_i}\partial_{w_i}$, so vanishing for the $w_i$ is vanishing for all of $S^W_+$. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The restriction $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\to C$ is an isomorphism of graded vector spaces because $\rho$ has kernel $I$ and $\mathcal H$ is a complement of $I$ by step 1.1; it is a map of $W$-modules because $\rho$ is $W$-equivariant. Hence $\dim\mathcal H_d=\dim C_d$ for every $d$, and $\dim\mathcal H=\dim C=|W|$ by [F2]. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $\varphi:S^W\otimes\mathcal H\to S$, $p\otimes h\mapsto ph$. This is a homomorphism of graded $S^W$-modules and of $W$-modules. Its reduction modulo $S^W_+$, namely $\mathcal H\to C$, $h\mapsto\rho(h)$, is surjective because it is the isomorphism $\rho|_{\mathcal H}$ of step 2.2. [step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 The map $\varphi$ is surjective: given homogeneous $f\in S_d$, choose $h\in\mathcal H_d$ with $\rho(f)=\rho(h)$ by step 3.1; then $f-h\in I_d=\sum_i(w_iS)_d=\sum_iw_iS_{d-2d_i}$, so by induction on $d$ each $w_ig$ with $g\in S_{d-2d_i}$ lies in $S^W\cdot\mathcal H$, and adding $h$ exhibits $f$ in the image. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The map $\varphi$ is injective: by steps 1.2 and 2.2 the two sides have the same Hilbert series, $$\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W\otimes\mathcal H,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal H,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t),$$ both are graded with finite-dimensional graded pieces, and by step 4.1 the kernel of the surjective graded $S^W$-linear map $\varphi$ would otherwise contribute positive Hilbert series. Hence $\varphi$ is an isomorphism. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Steps 2.1, 2.2 and 5.1 give a $W$-stable graded complement $\mathcal H$ of $I$ with $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\cong C$ and $S^W\otimes\mathcal H\cong S$; the description of $\mathcal H$ as the simultaneous invariant differential kernel follows from the adjointness $\langle pf,g\rangle=\langle f,\partial_{\overline p}g\rangle$ of step 1.1, and $\dim\mathcal H=|W|$ by step 2.2. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the invariant-theory suppliers [F1] and [F2]; the construction itself uses only finite averages and finite-dimensional linear algebra. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 5.1] ∎

Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published invariant-theory
items. Let $W$ act on the Cartan space $\mathfrak h$ by reflections and on
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$ by graded algebra automorphisms, with coinvariant algebra
$C=S/I$ as in [[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]]. Then there
is a $W$-stable graded subspace $\mathcal H\subseteq S$, finite dimensional of
dimension $|W|$, such that the multiplication map
$$S^W\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathcal H\longrightarrow S,\qquad p\otimes h\mapsto ph,$$
is an isomorphism of graded $S^W$-modules and of $W$-modules, and the
restriction of the quotient map $\rho:S\to C$ to $\mathcal H$ is an isomorphism
of graded $W$-modules $\mathcal H\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }C$. One may take
$$\mathcal H=\{f\in S:\partial_pf=0\text{ for all }p\in S^W_+\},$$
using constant-coefficient differential operators from a $W$-invariant
positive definite form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$. Any $W$-stable graded
complement of $I$ has the same multiplication and quotient properties. This
is the simultaneous kernel of all positive-degree invariant differential
operators, not in general the kernel of the quadratic Laplacian alone. In particular $\dim\mathcal H_d=\dim C_d$ for every $d$ and
$\sum_d\dim\mathcal H_d=|W|$.

Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Choose an arbitrary positive definite symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ and average it over the finite group $W$, obtaining a $W$-invariant positive definite form $(\ ,\ )$; choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\dots,e_r$ of $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ for it. For $p\in S$ let $\partial_p=p(\partial_1,\dots,\partial_r)$ be substitution of the partial derivatives $\partial_i=\partial/\partial e_i$; then multiplication by $p$ has adjoint $\partial_{\overline p}$, i.e. $\langle pf,g\rangle=\langle f,\partial_{\overline p}g\rangle$, as checked on monomials. Choose real basic invariants: real and imaginary parts of complex invariants are invariant, and one may choose a real homogeneous basis of the indecomposables of the invariant algebra and lift it; its complexification gives basic generators. Complex conjugation preserves $S^W_+$, so simultaneous kernels are unchanged. Set $\mathcal H_d:=I_d^{\perp}$ inside the finite-dimensional space $S_d$, and $\mathcal H:=\bigoplus_d\mathcal H_d$. source_claim_sections:
Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and Weyl group $W$,
and let $p_1,\dots,p_r$ be homogeneous basic generators of $S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}$
of degrees $d_1,\dots,d_r$, corresponding by Chevalley restriction to basic Weyl
invariants ([[thm-symmetric-invariants-restrict-to-weyl-invariants]],
[[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]]). Put
$$A=S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r).$$ Then $A$ is a reduced integral domain of
dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-r=2|\Phi^+|$, with Hilbert series
$$\operatorname{Hilb}(A,t)=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^r(1-t^{d_i})}{(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}},$$
and for every central character $\chi:Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to\mathbb C$ the PBW
associated graded of $U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$ is canonically
isomorphic to $A$.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $\mathfrak g=0$ then $r=0$ and $A=\mathbb C$, so all assertions hold; assume otherwise. By [F1], $S(\mathfrak g)$ is free over the polynomial invariant algebra $\mathbb C[p_1,\ldots,p_r]$. After quotienting by the first $j$ generators it remains free over $\mathbb C[p_{j+1},\ldots,p_r]$; hence multiplication by the next generator is injective and all successive quotients are nonzero. Thus the $p_i$ form a regular sequence, rather than merely a sequence of algebraically independent elements. The Koszul Euler characteristic gives $\operatorname{Hilb}(A,t)=\prod_i(1-t^{d_i})/(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}$. At any rational maximal ideal containing the $p_i$, the ambient polynomial local ring has dimension $\dim\mathfrak g$: the chain of translated coordinate ideals gives this lower bound at a rational point, and [[cor-dimension-of-a-finite-polynomial-ring-over-a-field]] gives the upper bound, and [F2] gives quotient dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-r$. At every prime the same regular sequence localizes and [F2] makes the quotient Cohen--Macaulay. In particular $\dim A=\dim\mathfrak g-r=2N$ by root-space decomposition. The Hilbert series has pole order $2N$ at $t=1$; it is not a polynomial of degree $2N$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Choose for every simple root $\alpha_i$ an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple $(e_i,f_i,h_i)$ and write $2\rho^\vee=\sum_i c_i h_i$ in the simple-coroot basis, so $\sum_i c_i\alpha_j(h_i)=2$ for every simple root $\alpha_j$, and put $e=\sum_i e_i$, $h=2\rho^\vee$, $f=\sum_i c_i f_i$. Distinct simple-root differences are not roots, so $[e_i,f_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$, and consequently $[h,e]=2e$, $[h,f]=-2f$ and $[e,f]=h$. The eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}h$ are $2\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$ and zero, hence all are even. Complete reducibility for this $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ subalgebra writes the adjoint module as a direct sum of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-strings $L(2m_1)\oplus\cdots$; each string contributes exactly one vector killed by $h$, and $\ker\operatorname{ad}h=\mathfrak h$ has dimension $r$, so there are exactly $r$ strings; a string with $m_j=0$ would consist of a nonzero vector killed by $e$ and $h$, i.e. a nonzero element of $\mathfrak h$ commuting with all $e_i$, which is central in $\mathfrak g$, hence zero; so all $m_j\ge1$ and counting dimensions gives $\sum_j(2m_j+1)=\dim\mathfrak g=2N+r$, that is $\sum_jm_j=N$. The highest vector of a string has $\operatorname{ad}h$-eigenvalue $2m_j>0$, hence lies in $\mathfrak n^+=\bigoplus_{\alpha>0}\mathfrak g_\alpha$; therefore $\ker\operatorname{ad}e$ is the $r$-dimensional span of the highest vectors and lies in $\mathfrak n^+$, and the lowest vectors span $z_f:=\ker\operatorname{ad}f\subseteq\mathfrak n^-$ with $\mathfrak g=[\mathfrak g,e]\oplus z_f$. [F3, algebra]

1.3 Let $\varphi_t(x)=t\cdot\operatorname{Ad}(t^{-\rho^\vee})(x)$ for $t\in\mathbb C^\times$. Since $p_i$ is $\mathfrak g$-invariant, $p_i(\varphi_tx)=t^{d_i}p_i(x)$ for all $x\in\mathfrak g$; since $\operatorname{Ad}(t^{-\rho^\vee})f_i=tf_i$, the map $\varphi_t$ preserves $z_f$, so with $q_i(y):=p_i(e+y)$ one has $q_i(\varphi_ty)=p_i(\varphi_t(e+y))=t^{d_i}q_i(y)$: each $q_i$ is weighted-homogeneous of weighted degree $d_i$ for the weights $\deg y_j=m_j+1$ on $z_f$; indeed a root vector of height $t$ has $\varphi$-weight $1-t$, so the lowest vector $y_j$ has weight $m_j+1\ge2$. [F3, algebra]

2.1 The group constructions needed below are explicit. Order the height spaces of $\mathfrak g$ by root height, with $\mathfrak h$ at height zero. The endomorphisms $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+$ strictly raise height. Exponential and logarithm are finite inverse polynomials on the corresponding strictly triangular matrices. For a unipotent automorphism $u$ which raises height relative to the identity, $\exp(t\log u)$ preserves the Lie bracket for every integer $t$ since it equals $u^t$; the bracket equations are polynomial in $t$, so they hold for all complex $t$. Differentiating at zero shows that $\log u$ is a derivation. By [F4] it equals $\operatorname{ad}x$; comparison of the height components shows $x\in\mathfrak n^+$, because negative-root components lower height and a Cartan component acts in height zero, and $\operatorname{ad}$ is injective. Thus $N_+=\exp(\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+)$ is exactly the closed subgroup of $G$ defined by these strict-height unipotence equations; it is polynomially isomorphic to $\mathfrak n^+$, hence connected. Let $H=(\mathbb C^\times)^r$ act by fixing $\mathfrak h$ and multiplying $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ by $\prod_i t_i^{a_i}$ when $\alpha=\sum_i a_i\alpha_i$. Root brackets show this is a closed torus of automorphisms, with Lie algebra $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak h$. It normalizes $N_+$; $B=HN_+$ is closed, since the diagonal entries determine its $H$ factor and the remaining strict-height unipotent equations determine its $N_+$ factor. It is connected and solvable, with Lie algebra $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak b$. Any Lie subalgebra containing $\mathfrak b$ is $\mathfrak h$-stable and splits into root spaces; if it is larger it contains a negative root space and hence, together with its positive root space, a root $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, so it cannot be solvable. Thus $B$ is maximal among connected solvable closed subgroups (a larger such subgroup would have larger solvable Lie algebra), and is a Borel. The connected group $G=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)^0$ is smooth and irreducible of dimension $\dim\mathfrak g$ by [F4], and its Borels are conjugate. These explicit tori also give the height scalings used in step 1.3. [F3, F4, algebra]

2.2 The central reduction has associated graded $A$: fix a central character $\chi:Z\to\mathbb C$ with kernel $\mathfrak m_\chi$, and let $J=\mathfrak m_\chi U(\mathfrak g)$. By [F6], $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)=S(\mathfrak g)$, $\operatorname{gr}Z=S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}$, and the leading symbol of any $z\in\mathfrak m_\chi$ lies in $S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}_+=(p_1,\dots,p_r)$; conversely each $p_i$ is the leading symbol of an element of $\mathfrak m_\chi$, for instance of $z_i-\chi(z_i)$ for a central element $z_i$ of leading symbol $p_i$ (the scalar term has lower filtration degree because $d_i>0$). Therefore $\operatorname{gr}J=(p_1,\dots,p_r)S(\mathfrak g)$ and the natural graded surjection $S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{gr}(U(\mathfrak g)/J)$ is an isomorphism: both sides have the Hilbert series of step 1.1, since the filtered free harmonic decomposition of [F6] restricts to a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)/J$ whose symbols have exactly the Hilbert series $\prod_i(1-t^{d_i})/(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}$. Hence the PBW associated graded of $U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$ is canonically $A$. [F6, step 1.1]

3.1 The morphism $\Psi:G\times z_f\to\mathfrak g$, $(g,y)\mapsto g\cdot(e+y)$, is dominant. Its differential at $(1,0)$ is $(\xi,y)\mapsto[\xi,e]+y$ for $\xi\in T_1G=\mathfrak g$ (using $G$-equivariance of the action), with image $[\mathfrak g,e]+z_f=\mathfrak g$ by step 1.2; hence the cotangent map is injective and, by the submersion criterion at the rational points $(1,0)$ and $e$, $\Psi$ is locally standard smooth, hence flat, at $(1,0)$; the flat locus is open and flat morphisms of finite presentation are open, so the image of $\Psi$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathfrak g$; since $\mathfrak g$ is irreducible, $\Psi$ is dominant. [F5, step 1.2, step 2.1]

3.2 If $\operatorname{ad}x$ is nilpotent, $U_x=\{\exp(t\operatorname{ad}x):t\in\mathbb C\}$ is a closed connected unipotent subgroup of $G$: for $x\ne0$ logarithm identifies it with the closed line $\mathbb C\operatorname{ad}x$; for $x=0$ it is trivial. Among connected solvable closed subgroups containing it choose one of maximal dimension; any strictly larger connected closed subgroup has larger dimension, so it is a Borel. Conjugacy from [F4] moves it into the $B$ constructed in step 2.1. Every unipotent element of that triangular group has diagonal entries all one, hence trivial $H$ factor, and lies in $N_+$. Its logarithm therefore belongs to $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+$ by step 2.1. Injectivity and equivariance of $\operatorname{ad}$ show that $x$ is conjugate into $\mathfrak n^+$. Conversely the invariant $p_i$ vanishes on $\mathfrak n^+$: the torus automorphism multiplying height $j$ by $t^j$ sends every $n\in\mathfrak n^+$ to zero as $t\to0$, while invariance preserves $p_i(n)$. Thus $p_i(n)=p_i(0)=0$. Lie invariance implies $G$-invariance here: the differential of $g\mapsto p_i(gx)$ vanishes on the connected smooth group, and in characteristic zero a regular function with zero differential on an irreducible variety is constant. [F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The restrictions $q_1,\dots,q_r\in\mathbb C[z_f]$ are algebraically independent: the pullback $\Psi^*$ is injective because $\Psi$ is dominant, and $\Psi^*(p_i)=q_i$ by $G$-invariance of the $p_i$; if a nonzero polynomial $F$ satisfied $F(q_1,\dots,q_r)=0$, then $\Psi^*(F(p_1,\dots,p_r))=0$, hence $F(p_1,\dots,p_r)=0$ in $S(\mathfrak g)$, contradicting the algebraic independence of $p_1,\dots,p_r$ from [F1]. [F1, step 3.1]

4.2 The common zero set $\mathcal N=\{x:p_i(x)=0\text{ for all }i\}$ equals $G\cdot\mathfrak n^+$: the inclusion $\supseteq$ is step 3.2, and conversely if all $p_i$ vanish then every invariant polynomial of positive degree vanishes, so the invariant traces $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{ad}x)^k)$, $k\ge1$, vanish because each is invariant with zero constant term; Newton's identities express every coefficient of the characteristic polynomial of $\operatorname{ad}x$ polynomially in these traces, so the characteristic polynomial is $T^{\dim\mathfrak g}$, hence $\operatorname{ad}x$ is nilpotent and $x$ is conjugate into $\mathfrak n^+$ by step 3.2. Also $\mathcal N$ is the underlying set of $\operatorname{Spec}A$. [F3, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 The map $q=(q_1,\dots,q_r):\mathbb A^r\to\mathbb A^r$ is dominant by step 4.1, and $\mathbb A^r$ is smooth, so generic smoothness provides a dense open subset of $\mathbb A^r$ on which the differential of $q$ is surjective; in particular the Jacobian determinant $D=\det(\partial q_i/\partial y_j)$ is not identically zero. [F5, step 4.1]

6.1 Weights: $D$ is weighted-homogeneous of weighted degree $\sum_id_i-\sum_j(m_j+1)=\sum_i(d_i-1)-\sum_jm_j=N-N=0$ by steps 1.2 and 1.3, because the derivative with respect to $y_j$ lowers weighted degree by $m_j+1$; a nonzero polynomial all of whose monomials have positive weights $m_j+1$ and total weighted degree zero is a nonzero constant. Hence $D$ is a nonzero constant, and in particular the linear map $z_f\to\mathbb C^r$, $y\mapsto(dp_1(e)(y),\dots,dp_r(e)(y))$, given by the matrix $(\partial q_i/\partial y_j)(0)$, is invertible. [step 1.2, step 1.3, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 The Jacobian matrix of the presentation $A=S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r)$ at the rational maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $e$ has rank exactly $r$: its rows are the differentials $dp_i(e)$, which are linearly independent by step 6.1. Since $\dim A_{\mathfrak m}=\dim A=\dim\mathfrak g-r$ by step 1.1, the Jacobian criterion in the form $\operatorname{rank}J(\mathfrak m)=n-\dim A_{\mathfrak m}$ identifies $A_{\mathfrak m}$ as a regular local ring. [F5, step 1.1, step 6.1]

8.1 The set $\mathcal N$ is irreducible: step 4.2 identifies its closed points with the image of the irreducible variety $G\times\mathfrak n^+$, so its closure is irreducible and equals the underlying space of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ ([[cor-closed-points-dense-in-affine-spectra]] and [[cor-weak-nullstellensatz-algebraically-closed-coordinate-form]] give density of its complex rational closed points). In particular there is a unique minimal prime $\mathfrak p_0$. The regular local ring $A_{\mathfrak m_e}$ of step 7.1 localizes further to $A_{\mathfrak p_0}$; localizations of regular local rings are regular by [[cor-localisations-of-regular-local-rings-are-regular]]. Since $\mathfrak p_0$ is minimal, that localization has dimension zero and is a field. This proves generic reducedness without needing an assertion about openness of the regular orbit. [F5, step 4.2, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 There are no embedded associated primes. For $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(A)$ choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\supseteq\mathfrak q$. An element with annihilator $\mathfrak q$ remains nonzero at $\mathfrak m$ and has annihilator $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak m}$, so this is an associated prime of $A_{\mathfrak m}$. That local ring is Cohen--Macaulay by step 1.1, and the associated-prime theorem in [F2] makes $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak m}$ minimal. Any strict smaller prime of $A$ below $\mathfrak q$ would remain strict after localization at $\mathfrak m$, so $\mathfrak q$ itself is minimal. Hence the only possible associated prime is the unique $\mathfrak p_0$ of step 8.1. The associated-localization detection map in [F5] therefore injects $A$ into the field $A_{\mathfrak p_0}$, proving that $A$ is an integral domain and in particular reduced. The Cohen--Macaulay argument is essential here; generic reducedness alone would not exclude embedded nilpotents. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 8.1, algebra]

10.1 Combining steps 1.1, 2.2, 9.1: $A$ is a reduced integral domain of dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-r=2N=2|\Phi^+|$ with the displayed Hilbert series, and every central reduction has associated graded $A$. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the invariant-theory, group-theoretic and geometric suppliers [F1], [F4], [F5] and [F6]; the conclusions themselves are choice-free statements about $\mathfrak g$. [F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 9.1, algebra] ∎

Proof

1.1 If $\mathfrak g=0$ then $r=0$ and $A=\mathbb C$, so all assertions hold; assume otherwise. By [F1], $S(\mathfrak g)$ is free over the polynomial invariant algebra $\mathbb C[p_1,\ldots,p_r]$. After quotienting by the first $j$ generators it remains free over $\mathbb C[p_{j+1},\ldots,p_r]$; hence multiplication by the next generator is injective and all successive quotients are nonzero. Thus the $p_i$ form a regular sequence, rather than merely a sequence of algebraically independent elements. The Koszul Euler characteristic gives $\operatorname{Hilb}(A,t)=\prod_i(1-t^{d_i})/(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}$. At any rational maximal ideal containing the $p_i$, the ambient polynomial local ring has dimension $\dim\mathfrak g$: the chain of translated coordinate ideals gives this lower bound at a rational point, and [[cor-dimension-of-a-finite-polynomial-ring-over-a-field]] gives the upper bound, and [F2] gives quotient dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-r$. At every prime the same regular sequence localizes and [F2] makes the quotient Cohen--Macaulay. In particular $\dim A=\dim\mathfrak g-r=2N$ by root-space decomposition. The Hilbert series has pole order $2N$ at $t=1$; it is not a polynomial of degree $2N$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Choose for every simple root $\alpha_i$ an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple $(e_i,f_i,h_i)$ and write $2\rho^\vee=\sum_i c_i h_i$ in the simple-coroot basis, so $\sum_i c_i\alpha_j(h_i)=2$ for every simple root $\alpha_j$, and put $e=\sum_i e_i$, $h=2\rho^\vee$, $f=\sum_i c_i f_i$. Distinct simple-root differences are not roots, so $[e_i,f_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$, and consequently $[h,e]=2e$, $[h,f]=-2f$ and $[e,f]=h$. The eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}h$ are $2\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$ and zero, hence all are even. Complete reducibility for this $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ subalgebra writes the adjoint module as a direct sum of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-strings $L(2m_1)\oplus\cdots$; each string contributes exactly one vector killed by $h$, and $\ker\operatorname{ad}h=\mathfrak h$ has dimension $r$, so there are exactly $r$ strings; a string with $m_j=0$ would consist of a nonzero vector killed by $e$ and $h$, i.e. a nonzero element of $\mathfrak h$ commuting with all $e_i$, which is central in $\mathfrak g$, hence zero; so all $m_j\ge1$ and counting dimensions gives $\sum_j(2m_j+1)=\dim\mathfrak g=2N+r$, that is $\sum_jm_j=N$. The highest vector of a string has $\operatorname{ad}h$-eigenvalue $2m_j>0$, hence lies in $\mathfrak n^+=\bigoplus_{\alpha>0}\mathfrak g_\alpha$; therefore $\ker\operatorname{ad}e$ is the $r$-dimensional span of the highest vectors and lies in $\mathfrak n^+$, and the lowest vectors span $z_f:=\ker\operatorname{ad}f\subseteq\mathfrak n^-$ with $\mathfrak g=[\mathfrak g,e]\oplus z_f$. [F3, algebra]

1.3 Let $\varphi_t(x)=t\cdot\operatorname{Ad}(t^{-\rho^\vee})(x)$ for $t\in\mathbb C^\times$. Since $p_i$ is $\mathfrak g$-invariant, $p_i(\varphi_tx)=t^{d_i}p_i(x)$ for all $x\in\mathfrak g$; since $\operatorname{Ad}(t^{-\rho^\vee})f_i=tf_i$, the map $\varphi_t$ preserves $z_f$, so with $q_i(y):=p_i(e+y)$ one has $q_i(\varphi_ty)=p_i(\varphi_t(e+y))=t^{d_i}q_i(y)$: each $q_i$ is weighted-homogeneous of weighted degree $d_i$ for the weights $\deg y_j=m_j+1$ on $z_f$; indeed a root vector of height $t$ has $\varphi$-weight $1-t$, so the lowest vector $y_j$ has weight $m_j+1\ge2$. [F3, algebra]

2.1 The group constructions needed below are explicit. Order the height spaces of $\mathfrak g$ by root height, with $\mathfrak h$ at height zero. The endomorphisms $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+$ strictly raise height. Exponential and logarithm are finite inverse polynomials on the corresponding strictly triangular matrices. For a unipotent automorphism $u$ which raises height relative to the identity, $\exp(t\log u)$ preserves the Lie bracket for every integer $t$ since it equals $u^t$; the bracket equations are polynomial in $t$, so they hold for all complex $t$. Differentiating at zero shows that $\log u$ is a derivation. By [F4] it equals $\operatorname{ad}x$; comparison of the height components shows $x\in\mathfrak n^+$, because negative-root components lower height and a Cartan component acts in height zero, and $\operatorname{ad}$ is injective. Thus $N_+=\exp(\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+)$ is exactly the closed subgroup of $G$ defined by these strict-height unipotence equations; it is polynomially isomorphic to $\mathfrak n^+$, hence connected. Let $H=(\mathbb C^\times)^r$ act by fixing $\mathfrak h$ and multiplying $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ by $\prod_i t_i^{a_i}$ when $\alpha=\sum_i a_i\alpha_i$. Root brackets show this is a closed torus of automorphisms, with Lie algebra $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak h$. It normalizes $N_+$; $B=HN_+$ is closed, since the diagonal entries determine its $H$ factor and the remaining strict-height unipotent equations determine its $N_+$ factor. It is connected and solvable, with Lie algebra $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak b$. Any Lie subalgebra containing $\mathfrak b$ is $\mathfrak h$-stable and splits into root spaces; if it is larger it contains a negative root space and hence, together with its positive root space, a root $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, so it cannot be solvable. Thus $B$ is maximal among connected solvable closed subgroups (a larger such subgroup would have larger solvable Lie algebra), and is a Borel. The connected group $G=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)^0$ is smooth and irreducible of dimension $\dim\mathfrak g$ by [F4], and its Borels are conjugate. These explicit tori also give the height scalings used in step 1.3. [F3, F4, algebra]

2.2 The central reduction has associated graded $A$: fix a central character $\chi:Z\to\mathbb C$ with kernel $\mathfrak m_\chi$, and let $J=\mathfrak m_\chi U(\mathfrak g)$. By [F6], $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)=S(\mathfrak g)$, $\operatorname{gr}Z=S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}$, and the leading symbol of any $z\in\mathfrak m_\chi$ lies in $S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}_+=(p_1,\dots,p_r)$; conversely each $p_i$ is the leading symbol of an element of $\mathfrak m_\chi$, for instance of $z_i-\chi(z_i)$ for a central element $z_i$ of leading symbol $p_i$ (the scalar term has lower filtration degree because $d_i>0$). Therefore $\operatorname{gr}J=(p_1,\dots,p_r)S(\mathfrak g)$ and the natural graded surjection $S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{gr}(U(\mathfrak g)/J)$ is an isomorphism: both sides have the Hilbert series of step 1.1, since the filtered free harmonic decomposition of [F6] restricts to a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)/J$ whose symbols have exactly the Hilbert series $\prod_i(1-t^{d_i})/(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}$. Hence the PBW associated graded of $U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$ is canonically $A$. [F6, step 1.1]

3.1 The morphism $\Psi:G\times z_f\to\mathfrak g$, $(g,y)\mapsto g\cdot(e+y)$, is dominant. Its differential at $(1,0)$ is $(\xi,y)\mapsto[\xi,e]+y$ for $\xi\in T_1G=\mathfrak g$ (using $G$-equivariance of the action), with image $[\mathfrak g,e]+z_f=\mathfrak g$ by step 1.2; hence the cotangent map is injective and, by the submersion criterion at the rational points $(1,0)$ and $e$, $\Psi$ is locally standard smooth, hence flat, at $(1,0)$; the flat locus is open and flat morphisms of finite presentation are open, so the image of $\Psi$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathfrak g$; since $\mathfrak g$ is irreducible, $\Psi$ is dominant. [F5, step 1.2, step 2.1]

3.2 If $\operatorname{ad}x$ is nilpotent, $U_x=\{\exp(t\operatorname{ad}x):t\in\mathbb C\}$ is a closed connected unipotent subgroup of $G$: for $x\ne0$ logarithm identifies it with the closed line $\mathbb C\operatorname{ad}x$; for $x=0$ it is trivial. Among connected solvable closed subgroups containing it choose one of maximal dimension; any strictly larger connected closed subgroup has larger dimension, so it is a Borel. Conjugacy from [F4] moves it into the $B$ constructed in step 2.1. Every unipotent element of that triangular group has diagonal entries all one, hence trivial $H$ factor, and lies in $N_+$. Its logarithm therefore belongs to $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+$ by step 2.1. Injectivity and equivariance of $\operatorname{ad}$ show that $x$ is conjugate into $\mathfrak n^+$. Conversely the invariant $p_i$ vanishes on $\mathfrak n^+$: the torus automorphism multiplying height $j$ by $t^j$ sends every $n\in\mathfrak n^+$ to zero as $t\to0$, while invariance preserves $p_i(n)$. Thus $p_i(n)=p_i(0)=0$. Lie invariance implies $G$-invariance here: the differential of $g\mapsto p_i(gx)$ vanishes on the connected smooth group, and in characteristic zero a regular function with zero differential on an irreducible variety is constant. [F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The restrictions $q_1,\dots,q_r\in\mathbb C[z_f]$ are algebraically independent: the pullback $\Psi^*$ is injective because $\Psi$ is dominant, and $\Psi^*(p_i)=q_i$ by $G$-invariance of the $p_i$; if a nonzero polynomial $F$ satisfied $F(q_1,\dots,q_r)=0$, then $\Psi^*(F(p_1,\dots,p_r))=0$, hence $F(p_1,\dots,p_r)=0$ in $S(\mathfrak g)$, contradicting the algebraic independence of $p_1,\dots,p_r$ from [F1]. [F1, step 3.1]

4.2 The common zero set $\mathcal N=\{x:p_i(x)=0\text{ for all }i\}$ equals $G\cdot\mathfrak n^+$: the inclusion $\supseteq$ is step 3.2, and conversely if all $p_i$ vanish then every invariant polynomial of positive degree vanishes, so the invariant traces $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{ad}x)^k)$, $k\ge1$, vanish because each is invariant with zero constant term; Newton's identities express every coefficient of the characteristic polynomial of $\operatorname{ad}x$ polynomially in these traces, so the characteristic polynomial is $T^{\dim\mathfrak g}$, hence $\operatorname{ad}x$ is nilpotent and $x$ is conjugate into $\mathfrak n^+$ by step 3.2. Also $\mathcal N$ is the underlying set of $\operatorname{Spec}A$. [F3, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 The map $q=(q_1,\dots,q_r):\mathbb A^r\to\mathbb A^r$ is dominant by step 4.1, and $\mathbb A^r$ is smooth, so generic smoothness provides a dense open subset of $\mathbb A^r$ on which the differential of $q$ is surjective; in particular the Jacobian determinant $D=\det(\partial q_i/\partial y_j)$ is not identically zero. [F5, step 4.1]

6.1 Weights: $D$ is weighted-homogeneous of weighted degree $\sum_id_i-\sum_j(m_j+1)=\sum_i(d_i-1)-\sum_jm_j=N-N=0$ by steps 1.2 and 1.3, because the derivative with respect to $y_j$ lowers weighted degree by $m_j+1$; a nonzero polynomial all of whose monomials have positive weights $m_j+1$ and total weighted degree zero is a nonzero constant. Hence $D$ is a nonzero constant, and in particular the linear map $z_f\to\mathbb C^r$, $y\mapsto(dp_1(e)(y),\dots,dp_r(e)(y))$, given by the matrix $(\partial q_i/\partial y_j)(0)$, is invertible. [step 1.2, step 1.3, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 The Jacobian matrix of the presentation $A=S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r)$ at the rational maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $e$ has rank exactly $r$: its rows are the differentials $dp_i(e)$, which are linearly independent by step 6.1. Since $\dim A_{\mathfrak m}=\dim A=\dim\mathfrak g-r$ by step 1.1, the Jacobian criterion in the form $\operatorname{rank}J(\mathfrak m)=n-\dim A_{\mathfrak m}$ identifies $A_{\mathfrak m}$ as a regular local ring. [F5, step 1.1, step 6.1]

8.1 The set $\mathcal N$ is irreducible: step 4.2 identifies its closed points with the image of the irreducible variety $G\times\mathfrak n^+$, so its closure is irreducible and equals the underlying space of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ ([[cor-closed-points-dense-in-affine-spectra]] and [[cor-weak-nullstellensatz-algebraically-closed-coordinate-form]] give density of its complex rational closed points). In particular there is a unique minimal prime $\mathfrak p_0$. The regular local ring $A_{\mathfrak m_e}$ of step 7.1 localizes further to $A_{\mathfrak p_0}$; localizations of regular local rings are regular by [[cor-localisations-of-regular-local-rings-are-regular]]. Since $\mathfrak p_0$ is minimal, that localization has dimension zero and is a field. This proves generic reducedness without needing an assertion about openness of the regular orbit. [F5, step 4.2, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 There are no embedded associated primes. For $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(A)$ choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\supseteq\mathfrak q$. An element with annihilator $\mathfrak q$ remains nonzero at $\mathfrak m$ and has annihilator $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak m}$, so this is an associated prime of $A_{\mathfrak m}$. That local ring is Cohen--Macaulay by step 1.1, and the associated-prime theorem in [F2] makes $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak m}$ minimal. Any strict smaller prime of $A$ below $\mathfrak q$ would remain strict after localization at $\mathfrak m$, so $\mathfrak q$ itself is minimal. Hence the only possible associated prime is the unique $\mathfrak p_0$ of step 8.1. The associated-localization detection map in [F5] therefore injects $A$ into the field $A_{\mathfrak p_0}$, proving that $A$ is an integral domain and in particular reduced. The Cohen--Macaulay argument is essential here; generic reducedness alone would not exclude embedded nilpotents. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 8.1, algebra]

10.1 Combining steps 1.1, 2.2, 9.1: $A$ is a reduced integral domain of dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-r=2N=2|\Phi^+|$ with the displayed Hilbert series, and every central reduction has associated graded $A$. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the invariant-theory, group-theoretic and geometric suppliers [F1], [F4], [F5] and [F6]; the conclusions themselves are choice-free statements about $\mathfrak g$. [F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 9.1, algebra] ∎

source_claim_sections:
Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a dominant regular integral representative
$\lambda$ and a reduced word $w=s_1\cdots s_k$, set
$\theta_{\underline w}=\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}$, so that the standards
follow right multiplication in word order. Then
$$\theta_{\underline w}\Delta(\lambda)\cong P(w\cdot\lambda)\oplus\bigoplus_{x<w}P(x\cdot\lambda)^{m_x},\qquad m_x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.$$
Its class is $(1+s_1)\cdots(1+s_k)$ under the standard class map, with actual
subexpression multiplicities. The BGG matrix satisfies
$(P(x\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=[\Delta(y\cdot\lambda):L(x\cdot\lambda)]$,
vanishes unless $y\le x$ in the Bruhat order, and has diagonal entries one.
Hence the top summand $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ occurs once and is the only summand
whose flag contains $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$; the remaining multiplicities are
determined by this triangular matrix and the product class. Consequently every
indecomposable projective is a summand of a word of wall crossings applied to
$\Delta(\lambda)$.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The object $Y:=\theta_{\underline w}\Delta(\lambda)$ is projective by [F1], and the block has finite-dimensional Hom spaces and finite decompositions, so $Y\cong\bigoplus_xP(x\cdot\lambda)^{m_x}$ with nonnegative multiplicities; its standard-flag multiplicities are read from its class in [F2], and every standard factor has a label $\le w$. [F1, F2]

2.1 No summand $P(x\cdot\lambda)$ with $x\not\le w$ occurs: the diagonal entry of the BGG matrix gives $(P(x\cdot\lambda):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))=1$ by [F3], so such a summand would contribute a standard factor $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ to $Y$ with $x\not\le w$, contradicting step 1.1. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 The full subexpression contributes $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ with multiplicity one to the product class, and no other summand $P(x\cdot\lambda)$ with $x\le w$, $x\neq w$ contributes to the multiplicity of $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$: $(P(x\cdot\lambda):\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))\neq0$ forces $w\le x$ by [F3], so with $x\le w$ it forces $x=w$. Hence $m_w=1$, and the only summand whose flag contains $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ is $P(w\cdot\lambda)$. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 The remaining multiplicities $m_x$, $x<w$, are determined recursively from the product class: the coefficient of $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ in the class of $Y$ equals $m_x+\sum_{x<z}m_z(P(z\cdot\lambda):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))$, whose second term involves only strictly larger labels already determined; solving downward in the finite Bruhat order gives all $m_x$. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Every indecomposable projective is a summand of such a word: the decomposition of step 1.1 with diagonal support realizes each $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ as a summand of $\theta_{\underline w}\Delta(\lambda)$ for any reduced word $w$, which is the stated generation statement. [step 3.1] ∎

reviews.disposition: The word of wall crossings yields a projective decomposition with a uniquely occurring top standard label. The statement is a decomposition and generation assertion, not an equivalence characterizing all functors.

source_claim_sections:
Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published items. Let
$\theta_s$ be the wall-crossing functor of
[[def-wall-crossing-functor-and-unit-counit]] attached to the simple reflection
$s$ in the regular integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$. For every $w\in W$ the
object $\theta_s\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ has a finite Verma flag with exactly two
factors, namely $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ and $\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)$, each with
multiplicity one; in the Grothendieck group
$$[\theta_s\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]=[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)].$$
Moreover $\theta_s$ is exact and preserves Verma-filtered objects with finite
Verma flags: if $X$ has a finite Verma flag with multiplicities
$(X:\Delta(v\cdot\lambda))$, then $\theta_sX$ has one with multiplicities
$(\theta_sX:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))=(X:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))+(X:\Delta(us\cdot\lambda))$,
and the same formula holds in $K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$. The resulting flag is
not in general split; splitting is neither asserted nor used.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 $\theta_s\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong T_{\mathrm{out}}\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$ by the first clause of [F1], hence it has the two-factor finite Verma flag of the second clause of [F1] with factors $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ and $\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)$, each once; its class in $K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$ is $[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)]$ by [F2]. [F1, F2]

2.1 Let $X$ be Verma-filtered with finite flag $0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$ and factors $\Delta(v_i\cdot\lambda)$. Exactness of $\theta_s$ by [F2] makes $0=\theta_sX_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\theta_sX_n=\theta_sX$ an increasing chain of subobjects, and each quotient $\theta_sX_i/\theta_sX_{i-1}\cong\theta_s(X_i/X_{i-1})\cong\theta_s\Delta(v_i\cdot\lambda)$ carries the two-factor flag of step 1.1; concatenating these two-step flags through the chain yields a finite Verma flag of $\theta_sX$ with factor multiplicities $(X:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))+(X:\Delta(us\cdot\lambda))$, where the independence of the flag [F2] makes the count well defined. [F2, step 1.1]

Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published items. Let

source_claim_sections:
Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published items. In the
regular integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$ of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]] the
assignment
$$c\colon K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z[W],\qquad[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]\longmapsto w,$$
is an isomorphism of abelian groups, and for every simple reflection $s$ the
wall-crossing functor $\theta_s$ of
[[def-wall-crossing-functor-and-unit-counit]] satisfies
$$c\,[\theta_sX]=c\,[X]\cdot(1+s)\qquad\text{for all }X\in\mathcal O_\lambda,$$
right multiplication by $1+s$ in the integral group ring $\mathbb Z[W]$.
Consequently, for a reduced word $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ one has
$$c\,[\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}\Delta(\lambda)]=(1+s_1)(1+s_2)\cdots(1+s_k),$$
the sum of all subexpression products with their actual multiplicities; its top
Bruhat term is $w$ once and all other terms have strictly smaller labels. With
the composition $\theta_{s_1}\cdots\theta_{s_k}$ instead, the factors are
multiplied in the reverse order.
source_proof_sections:
Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The map $c$ is a well-defined homomorphism: by [F1] the classes of the standards are a $\mathbb Z$-basis indexed by the $|W|$ elements of $W$; sending the basis element $[\Delta(v\cdot\lambda)]$ to $v$ therefore extends uniquely to an isomorphism of free abelian groups of rank $|W|$. [F1]

2.1 On every Verma class the formula holds: $c[\theta_s\Delta(v\cdot\lambda)]=v+vs=v(1+s)=c[\Delta(v\cdot\lambda)]\cdot(1+s)$ by [F2], using that right multiplication by $s$ in $\mathbb Z[W]$ sends the basis element $v$ to $vs$. Since $\theta_s$ is exact by [F2] it induces an additive endomorphism of $K_0$; agreement on the standard basis [F1] gives $c[\theta_sX]=c[X](1+s)$ for all $X\in\mathcal O_\lambda$, and both sides are additive in $X$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Iterate step 2.1 along the word, applying the factors in the order in which they act: the composite $\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}$ applies $\theta_{s_1}$ first, so $c[\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}\Delta(\lambda)]=(((1+s_1))(1+s_2))\cdots(1+s_k)=(1+s_1)(1+s_2)\cdots(1+s_k)$; expanding the product gives the sum over all subwords $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_r}$, $i_1<\cdots<i_r$, of their products, with the multiplicity with which each product arises. The full subword contributes $w$ once; every proper subword has strictly smaller length, and its product is $\le w$ with smaller length, hence strictly smaller than $w$ in the Bruhat order by [F3]. Reversing the order of composition multiplies the factors in the reverse order, as recorded. [F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
